easy.prompt: A town's household incomes have mean $85,000 and median $60,000. What shape does this suggest?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Right-skewed, with a tail of high earners

choices.label: B
choices.body: Left-skewed, with a tail of low earners

easy.hint: Next step: compare mean vs median — the mean follows the tail.
easy.explanation: Mean above median means high values pull the average up, so the tail stretches right.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Median 60k marks the middle household. Step 2: Mean 85k sits 25k above it, so extremes must be on the high side. Step 3: A few very high incomes (say three $500k earners among 100 households) add about $15k to the mean but barely move the median. Step 4: That pattern is the signature of right skew.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Low tail would drag the mean below the median, but here mean exceeds median.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Symmetric data would put mean and median within sampling noise of each other.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Uniform data would still have mean near median, not 25k apart.

easy.prompt: Exam scores cluster near 90 with a few scores down at 30-40, and the mean is below the median. What shape is this?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Left-skewed, with a tail of low scores

choices.label: C
choices.body: Right-skewed, with a tail of high scores

easy.hint: Next step: ask which side the stragglers sit on — that side holds the tail.
easy.explanation: A cluster at the top with low stragglers is a left tail, and the mean sinks below the median.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Most scores near 90 anchor the median high. Step 2: Just five scores of 30 in a class of 40 drag the total down by roughly 300 points, about 7.5 points off the mean. Step 3: The median ignores how far those five fall, so mean < median. Step 4: Mean below median with low extremes defines left skew.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: A symmetric mound would keep mean and median together, not mean below median.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: High tail would lift the mean above the median, the reverse of this data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Two equal peaks would show two clusters, not one cluster plus stragglers.

easy.prompt: Incomes in a neighborhood are heavily right-skewed by a few very high earners. Which center best describes a typical household?
easy.hint: Next step: ask which center resists extremes — the middle value ignores how far the tail reaches.
easy.explanation: The median is the middle household and barely moves when top incomes soar; the mean follows them.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Take 9 households at $50k plus one at $1.05M. Step 2: The median is $50k either way. Step 3: The mean is ($450k + $1,050k)/10 = $150k, triple the typical household. Step 4: So for skewed income the median reports the typical case honestly.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: A few huge incomes inflate the mean far above any typical household here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Range measures spread from min to max, not a center.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Standard deviation measures spread around the mean, not a center.

easy.prompt: Birth weights of healthy full-term babies are roughly symmetric with no outliers. Which center is appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Median only; the mean is forbidden

choices.label: B
choices.body: Mean, since symmetry makes it efficient and unbiased

choices.label: C
choices.body: Mode only, ignoring all other values

easy.hint: Next step: check symmetry and outliers — with neither problem, the mean uses all data well.
easy.explanation: For symmetric outlier-free data the mean equals the median and uses every value efficiently.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: With 100 weights centered near 3.4 kg and SD 0.4 kg, mean and median both land near 3.40 kg. Step 2: No tail pulls either one away. Step 3: The mean averages all 100 values, giving SE about 0.04 kg. Step 4: So the mean is a fine, slightly more efficient default here.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Nothing forbids the mean when data are symmetric without outliers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The mode wastes nearly all information in continuous data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The maximum is an extreme, not a center.

easy.prompt: The interquartile range (IQR) equals…
easy.hint: Next step: picture the box — IQR is the width of the middle-50% box.
easy.explanation: IQR spans the middle half of the data, from the first to the third quartile.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Order the data and cut it into quarters. Step 2: With Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 40, the middle 50% stretches across 20 units. Step 3: So IQR = 40 − 20 = 20. Step 4: Adding quartiles or using min/max answers a different question.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Adding quartiles gives a location-like sum, not a spread.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Max minus min is the full range, which includes the extreme quarters the IQR trims.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Mean minus median measures skew direction, not the width of the middle half.

easy.prompt: In a boxplot, the left and right edges of the box and the line inside it represent…
easy.hint: Next step: read the box from outside in — edges are quartiles, the divider is the middle value.
easy.explanation: Box edges mark the quartiles enclosing the middle 50%, and the inside line is the median.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: With Q1 = 20, median = 30, Q3 = 40, the box spans 20 to 40. Step 2: The line at 30 splits the box into lower and upper quarters of the data. Step 3: Whiskers then reach toward min and max (or fences). Step 4: So one glance gives five-number-summary landmarks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Mean and SD are not plotted as box landmarks in a standard boxplot.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Min and max sit at whisker tips, not box edges; the line is the median, not the mean.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The inside divider is the median; the mean is not marked by default.

easy.prompt: With Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 40, the 1.5×IQR upper fence flags high outliers above…
easy.hint: Next step: compute IQR first, then reach 1.5 IQRs above Q3.
easy.explanation: IQR is 20, so the fence is 40 + 1.5(20) = 70.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: IQR = 40 − 20 = 20. Step 2: Multiply: 1.5 × 20 = 30. Step 3: Add to Q3: 40 + 30 = 70. Step 4: Values above 70 (e.g., 85) get flagged as high outliers.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 50 adds only 0.5 IQR to Q3, not 1.5.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 60 adds just 1 IQR to Q3.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 80 adds 2 IQR to Q3, overshooting the 1.5 rule.

easy.prompt: A z-score of −1.5 for an observation means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The value is 1.5 units below zero

choices.label: B
choices.body: The value is 1.5 SD above the mean

choices.label: C
choices.body: The value is 1.5 SD below the mean

easy.hint: Next step: decode z as (value − mean)/SD — sign gives side, size gives SDs.
easy.explanation: Negative z sits below the mean by 1.5 standard deviations.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: With mean 100 and SD 10, z = −1.5 gives x = 100 + (−1.5)(10) = 85. Step 2: 85 is 15 units, i.e., 1.5 SDs, below 100. Step 3: The sign only orients (below), the 1.5 scales. Step 4: So z = −1.5 always means 1.5 SDs under center.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: z is relative to the mean in SD units, not to zero in raw units.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Above the mean needs positive z; the sign here is negative.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: z is a standardized position, not a probability.

easy.prompt: A drug beats placebo in Ward X (60% vs 50%) and in Ward Y (90% vs 80%), yet pooled over both wards it looks worse. How is this possible?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Arithmetic error; pooling can never reverse

choices.label: B
choices.body: Wards differ in size and baseline risk, so the mix confounds the pooled rate

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only the pooled rate is ever valid

easy.hint: Next step: check where each group's patients went — uneven ward mixes tilt the average.
easy.explanation: Different patient mixes per ward confound the pooled comparison even when each ward favors the drug.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Suppose the drug arm holds 90 severe Ward-X patients at 60% plus 10 mild Ward-Y patients at 90%: pooled (54+9)/100 = 63%. Step 2: Placebo holds 10 Ward-X at 50% plus 90 Ward-Y at 80%: pooled (5+72)/100 = 77%. Step 3: Each ward favors the drug (+10 points), yet pooled placebo wins by 14 points. Step 4: The ward mix, not efficacy, flipped the verdict — the drug arm drew the harder patients.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: This is Simpson's paradox; unequal mixing genuinely reverses pooled rates.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: When groups differ, pooled rates can mislead and stratified rates rule.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Subgroup rates are exactly what unmask the confounding here.

easy.prompt: If P(A) = 0.42 for a simple event A, what is P(not A)?
easy.hint: Next step: use the complement rule — something either happens or it doesn't.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: A and not-A split all possibilities with no overlap. Step 2: Their probabilities must total 1. Step 3: So 1 − 0.42 = 0.58. Step 4: Out of 100 repeats, A occurs ~42 times and fails ~58 times.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's P(A) itself, not its complement.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Probabilities can never exceed 1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Halving applies to nothing in the complement rule.

easy.prompt: Events A and B are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.2. What is P(A or B)?
easy.hint: Next step: check overlap — mutually exclusive means no overlap to subtract.
easy.explanation: With no overlap, P(A ∪ B) = 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.5.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Mutually exclusive means both cannot co-occur, so P(A∩B) = 0. Step 2: Addition rule: 0.3 + 0.2 − 0 = 0.5. Step 3: In 100 trials expect ~30 A-only plus ~20 B-only. Step 4: Neither-overlap nor double-counting enters here.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Multiplying is for independent intersections, not exclusive unions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Subtracting applies when overlap exists; here overlap is zero.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Probabilities total 1 only across a full partition, not two events.

easy.prompt: A standard deck has 52 cards with 12 face cards (J/Q/K). What is P(face card on one draw)?
easy.hint: Next step: count favorables over equally likely cards.
easy.explanation: 12 face cards out of 52 equally likely cards gives 12/52 = 3/13.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: 4 suits × 3 face ranks = 12 favorables. Step 2: 52 total equally likely outcomes. Step 3: 12/52 simplifies to 3/13 ≈ 0.23. Step 4: About 23 draws in 100 show a face card.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 1/13 is one rank (e.g., kings), not all three face ranks.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Half the deck is not face cards — only 12 of 52.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 26 is half a deck, not the deck size.

easy.prompt: Events A and B are independent. Which identity holds?
easy.hint: Next step: recall what independence means — B's occurrence doesn't change A's odds.
easy.explanation: Independence means the joint factorizes into the product of marginals.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Independence says P(A|B) = P(A). Step 2: Since P(A∩B) = P(A|B)P(B), substitution gives P(A)P(B). Step 3: With P(A)=0.4, P(B)=0.5, joint = 0.2. Step 4: No subtraction or equality of marginals is involved.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That omits the overlap term unless events are mutually exclusive.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Zero conditional means incompatibility, the opposite of independence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Equal probabilities are never required for independence.

easy.prompt: Disease prevalence is 2%. A test has 99% sensitivity and 95% specificity. Roughly what is P(disease | positive)?
easy.hint: Next step: weigh true positives against false positives in a big imaginary crowd.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: In 10,000 people, 200 are sick; test catches ~198. Step 2: Of 9,800 healthy, 5% (≈490) falsely test positive. Step 3: Positives total 198+490 = 688, of which 198/688 ≈ 28.8% are sick. Step 4: Most positives are healthy because the disease is rare — the base rate rules.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's sensitivity P(+|disease), the reverse conditional.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's specificity among the healthy, not the posterior.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's the prior before seeing the test result.

easy.prompt: The law of large numbers says that as sample size grows, the sample mean…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Tends to get closer to the population mean

easy.hint: Next step: think stability — averaging washes out individual noise.
easy.explanation: Averaging stabilizes around the true mean for independent, identically distributed data.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: One die roll averages anywhere 1-6 (SD ≈ 1.7). Step 2: Mean of 100 rolls has SE ≈ 0.17. Step 3: Mean of 10,000 rolls has SE ≈ 0.017, hugging 3.5. Step 4: Convergence is probabilistic tightening, not an exact n=30 switch.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: No fixed n forces exact equality; closeness is gradual and chancy.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Variability of the mean shrinks like 1/√n, not grows.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Mean and median differ whenever skew exists.

easy.prompt: Two polls of 1,000 voters each show 48% and 52% support. What best explains the gap?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Ordinary sampling variation: SE ≈ 1.6 points, so ±4 gaps are common

easy.hint: Next step: compute the standard error of each poll before crying foul.
easy.explanation: SE = √(0.5·0.5/1000) ≈ 1.6 points, so a 4-point split is routine noise.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Each poll's SE ≈ √(0.25/1000) ≈ 0.0158. Step 2: Difference SE ≈ 1.58·√2 ≈ 2.2 points. Step 3: A 4-point gap is under 2 SEs — expected fairly often. Step 4: Disagreement within ~±4.4 points needs no misconduct story.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Noise alone produces such splits regularly; fraud is unevidenced.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No time-travel needed — simultaneous polls still vary.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Random samples vary by design; exact repeats would be suspicious.

easy.prompt: A fair coin landed heads 5 times in a row. What is P(heads on the next flip)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Much less than 1/2; tails is due

easy.hint: Next step: ask what the coin remembers — flips are independent.
easy.explanation: Each flip is independent with P(H) = 1/2 regardless of history.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Independence means P(H | HHHHH) = P(H). Step 2: The coin's physics reset every toss. Step 3: 5-heads runs occur ~3 times per 100 six-flip windows — unsurprising. Step 4: 'Due' tails would require the coin to track history, which it cannot.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Balance happens via dilution over thousands of flips, not compensation next flip.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No momentum exists; P(HHHHHH) = 1/64 was fixed before flipping began.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Six-head runs happen with probability 1/64 — rare but real.

easy.prompt: A basketball player makes 80% of free throws. What is P(missing one random attempt)?
easy.hint: Next step: make-or-miss covers everything — subtract from 1.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Each attempt is make or miss, partitioning 100%. Step 2: 80 of 100 attempts swish. Step 3: The other 20 of 100 miss. Step 4: 20/100 = 0.20.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's P(make), the complement of what's asked.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Probabilities cannot exceed 1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Halving the miss rate has no basis here.

easy.prompt: A sample has s = 10 with n = 25. What is the standard error of the mean?
easy.hint: Next step: divide s by the square root of n, not by n.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: √n = √25 = 5. Step 2: Divide spread by 5: 10/5 = 2. Step 3: So sample means vary by ~2 around μ. Step 4: With n = 100 the SE would halve again to 1.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's s itself; the mean of 25 varies less than individuals.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's s/n, which shrinks far too fast.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's √n, the divisor, not the result.

easy.prompt: A sample has s = 12 with n = 36. What is the standard error of the mean?
easy.hint: Next step: take √36 first, then divide.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: √36 = 6. Step 2: 12/6 = 2. Step 3: Means of 36 scatter ~2 units around μ versus 12 for individuals. Step 4: Quadrupling to n = 144 would halve SE to 1.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's s, the individual-level spread, not the mean's.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's s/n ≈ 0.33, dividing by n instead of √n.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's √n, not s/√n.

easy.prompt: Incomes are right-skewed, but n = 400 workers are sampled. What does the CLT say about x̄?

choices.label: A
choices.body: x̄ is exactly normal for any n

choices.label: B
choices.body: x̄'s sampling distribution is approximately normal

easy.hint: Next step: separate the data's shape from the mean's shape — CLT speaks about the mean.
easy.explanation: CLT: the distribution of x̄ approaches normal as n grows, even from skewed data.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Individual incomes stay skewed — CLT never reshapes the sample. Step 2: But x̄ averages 400 independent draws, SE = σ/20. Step 3: At n = 400 that average's distribution is bell-shaped around μ. Step 4: So z-intervals for the mean work despite skew.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Approximately, not exactly — and largeness is required.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The sample keeps its skew; only the mean's distribution symmetrizes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Mean and median still differ under skew.

easy.prompt: Which condition matters for CLT-based intervals for a mean?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Data must be perfectly normal at any n

choices.label: B
choices.body: Roughly independent observations with finite variance and large-enough n

easy.hint: Next step: list what CLT actually assumes — independence, finite spread, enough n.
easy.explanation: CLT needs near-independence, finite variance, and n big enough for the skew at hand.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Independence lets variances add (SE = σ/√n). Step 2: Finite variance keeps σ/√n meaningful. Step 3: n = 30 suffices for mild skew; heavy skew needs more. Step 4: Perfect normality is never required — that myth defeats the theorem's purpose.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: CLT's point is handling non-normal data via large n.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 30 is a guideline, not a magic number.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Infinite populations are the textbook default; finiteness adds corrections.

easy.prompt: In n = 200 with true p = 0.20, what is the SE of the sample proportion?
easy.hint: Next step: plug into √(p(1−p)/n).
easy.deepDive: Step 1: p(1−p) = 0.2×0.8 = 0.16. Step 2: Divide by 200: 0.0008. Step 3: Square root: ≈ 0.0283 (2.8 points). Step 4: So p̂ lands within ±5.6 points of p ~95% of the time.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's p itself, not its sampling variability.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's the variance numerator p(1−p), before dividing by n and rooting.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's roughly the variance 0.0008 rounded, missing the square root.

easy.prompt: What is one bootstrap replicate for estimating the median?

choices.label: B
choices.body: A resample of size n drawn WITH replacement from the data

choices.label: C
choices.body: A new random sample from the population

easy.hint: Next step: mimic sampling by re-drawing from what you have — with replacement.
easy.explanation: Bootstrap treats the sample as a stand-in population and resamples it with replacement.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Original n = 50 incomes. Step 2: Draw 50 with replacement: some repeat, some omitted. Step 3: Compute that replicate's median. Step 4: Repeat 1000×; the middle 95% of medians is the interval.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Sorting computes one median; bootstrap needs thousands of resampled medians.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: New population sampling is impossible — the sample is all we have.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Deleting outliers biases the stand-in population.

easy.prompt: What is a sampling distribution?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A histogram of one sample's raw values

choices.label: B
choices.body: The distribution of a statistic across all possible samples of size n

choices.label: D
choices.body: A list of every population member

easy.hint: Next step: shift focus from individuals to the statistic — imagine repeating the whole survey.
easy.explanation: Sampling distribution = what x̄ (or p̂) does over repeated samples.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: One sample of 100 gives a single x̄ = $62k. Step 2: Repeat 1000 times: 1000 x̄ values scatter ~σ/10 around μ. Step 3: That scatter's shape is the sampling distribution. Step 4: It is narrower and more normal than the raw-income histogram.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's the sample distribution — one realization's raw spread.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The population is fixed; the sampling distribution describes statistics computed from it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's a census roster, not a distribution of a statistic.

easy.prompt: CLT says means become near-normal for large n 'regardless of population shape'. What does this assume?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Any data, even dependent or infinite-variance

choices.label: B
choices.body: Roughly independent draws with finite variance

easy.hint: Next step: read the fine print — textbook CLT needs independence plus finite variance.
easy.explanation: Mild conditions: near-independence and finite σ²; shape itself is free.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Finite variance gives SE = σ/√n meaning. Step 2: Independence lets variances add across draws. Step 3: Cauchy (infinite variance) breaks it: x̄ stays Cauchy at any n. Step 4: So 'any shape' means any finite-variance shape, not literally anything.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Dependence and infinite variance are the two classic breakers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Cauchy x̄ never normalizes — the canonical counterexample.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Trends violate identical-distribution; de-trend first.

easy.prompt: For random samples of size n from population mean μ, what is the mean of x̄'s sampling distribution?
easy.hint: Next step: average the averages — unbiasedness means they center on μ.
easy.explanation: E[x̄] = μ: the sampling distribution centers exactly on the population mean.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: With μ = $60k, one x̄ might be $58k, another $63k. Step 2: Over all possible samples they average $60k. Step 3: No √n scaling touches the center — only the spread. Step 4: That's why x̄ is unbiased for μ.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: √n shrinks spread, never the center.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Multiplying by √n would claim $60k·5 = $300k — absurd.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Zero is the mean of z-scores, not of x̄.

easy.prompt: A 95% confidence interval for a population mean is correctly interpreted as: if we repeated sampling many times and built intervals the same way…

choices.label: A
choices.body: About 95% of those intervals would contain the true mean

choices.label: B
choices.body: 95% of individual observations fall inside each interval

choices.label: C
choices.body: There is a 95% chance each single computed interval is wrong

choices.label: D
choices.body: The next sample mean will land inside with certainty

easy.hint: Next step: ask WHO varies — the intervals dance, the true mean stands still.
easy.explanation: Coverage is a long-run property of the procedure, not a description of one dataset's spread.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Fix μ = 100; draw 1000 samples of n = 36. Step 2: Each gives its own x̄ ± 2SE interval. Step 3: ~950 of the 1000 trap μ; ~50 miss. Step 4: So '95% confident' describes the method's hit rate, not a guarantee for interval #7.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That describes a prediction/tolerance band for individuals, not a CI for μ.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Inverted: ~95% of intervals are right, ~5% wrong.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: x̄ varies too; the next mean has ~95% chance only in the procedure sense, never certainty.

easy.prompt: A 95% CI for mean birth weight is (3.2 kg, 3.6 kg). Which claim is WRONG?

choices.label: A
choices.body: We are 95% confident the true mean lies between 3.2 and 3.6 kg

choices.label: B
choices.body: 95% of babies weigh between 3.2 and 3.6 kg

choices.label: C
choices.body: The sample mean was 3.4 kg (the midpoint)

choices.label: D
choices.body: Repeating the study would give a slightly different interval

easy.hint: Next step: compare widths — a CI for μ is far narrower than the babies' spread.
easy.explanation: The interval traps the mean (~SE wide), while individual weights scatter ~SD wide.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: With s = 0.5 kg, n = 100, SE = 0.05 kg and the CI spans 0.4 kg. Step 2: Individuals span roughly 3.4 ± 1.0 kg (±2 SD). Step 3: Claiming 95% of babies sit in a 0.4 kg window confuses SE with SD. Step 4: The midpoint 3.4 kg is x̄, and reruns would shift it by ~SE each time.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is the standard confidence phrasing — correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Symmetric CIs center on x̄ = 3.4 kg — correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sampling variation moves x̄ run to run — correct.

easy.prompt: All else equal, increasing sample size n makes a confidence interval for μ…
easy.hint: Next step: trace n through the margin — SE = s/√n shrinks.
easy.explanation: Standard error σ/√n falls as n grows, shrinking the margin of error.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: n = 25, s = 10: SE = 2, margin ≈ 4.1. Step 2: n = 100: SE = 1, margin ≈ 2.0. Step 3: Width halves while confidence stays 95%. Step 4: More data buys precision, not bias removal.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Larger n adds information and tightens the interval.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Margin of error explicitly depends on n via SE.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Larger samples are preferred for precision.

easy.prompt: You have x̄ = 120, s = 15, n = 36. What is the standard error s/√n?
easy.hint: Next step: √36 first, then divide.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: √36 = 6. Step 2: 15/6 = 2.5. Step 3: Sample means scatter ~2.5 around μ. Step 4: The 95% margin will be about ±5 (2×SE).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's s, not SE.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's s/n, not s/√n.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's √n, the divisor.

easy.prompt: A poll finds 40 successes in 200 trials. What is p̂?
easy.hint: Next step: divide successes by trials.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: 40 of 200 support. Step 2: 40/200 = 1/5 = 0.20. Step 3: About 20% support in-sample. Step 4: (0.16 would be p̂(1−p̂), a variance piece — not asked.)

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's 40/100 — wrong denominator.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's 4/200 — misplaced decimal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's p̂(1−p̂) = 0.16, the variance numerator, not p̂.

easy.prompt: A two-sample interval estimates…

choices.label: B
choices.body: μ₁ − μ₂ (the difference of population means)

easy.hint: Next step: ask what comparison the study wants — group 1 minus group 2.
easy.explanation: Two-sample inference targets the gap between means, e.g., drug minus placebo.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: x̄₁ = 52, x̄₂ = 47: point estimate 5. Step 2: The CI (say −0.7 to 10.7) brackets the true gap. Step 3: It does not describe individuals in either group. Step 4: One-sample intervals would trap each μ separately instead.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Sums are rarely of interest; differences compare.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Individuals vary ~SD wide; the gap's SE is far tighter.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sample size enters SE, but is never the target.

easy.prompt: In a paired (before/after) design, the CI is built on…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The two group means separately, ignoring pairs

choices.label: B
choices.body: The within-pair differences, as a one-sample t on d

easy.hint: Next step: collapse each pair to one number — after minus before.
easy.explanation: Pairing turns 2n correlated values into n independent differences.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Pair (140, 132) → d = −8; repeat for all 36 patients. Step 2: d̄ = −6, sd = 9: SE = 9/6 = 1.5. Step 3: CI: −6 ± 2.03(1.5) = (−9.0, −3.0). Step 4: Analyzing groups separately would waste the pairing and inflate SE.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Ignoring pairs discards the design's variance-removal power.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Sums keep between-person noise; differences cancel it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 'After' alone confounds treatment with baseline.

easy.prompt: Which conditions support a one-sample t-interval for μ?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Random sample + near-normal population or large n

easy.hint: Next step: check the two gates — how data were gathered, and whether x̄ is near-normal.
easy.explanation: Randomness licenses generalization; normality-or-large-n licenses the t curve.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Random n = 40 incomes (skewed): x̄ near-normal by CLT — OK. Step 2: n = 8 skewed: x̄ still skewed — not OK. Step 3: Convenience samples generalize only with extra assumptions. Step 4: Uniformity is never required.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Convenience sampling biases toward the reachable subgroup.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: n = 2 under skew gives a wildly non-t x̄.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Any shape works given enough n — uniform has no privilege.

easy.prompt: What does '95% coverage' mean for a CI method?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 95% of the data fall inside each interval

choices.label: B
choices.body: About 95% of intervals from repeated samples trap the parameter

choices.label: C
choices.body: The parameter moves 95% of the time

easy.hint: Next step: repeat the study in your head — the method's hit rate is the coverage.
easy.explanation: Long-run trapping rate over reruns, not data percentage inside one interval.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Simulate 10,000 samples, build 10,000 intervals. Step 2: ~9,500 contain μ. Step 3: 9,500/10,000 = 95% coverage. Step 4: Any single interval just is or isn't covering.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's a prediction-interval reading — wrong target.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The parameter is fixed; intervals vary.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: p-values are separate machinery.

easy.prompt: A p-value is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The probability H₀ is true after seeing data

choices.label: B
choices.body: The probability, assuming H₀ is true, of data at least as extreme as observed

easy.hint: Next step: condition on H₀ — the p-value assumes the null, then judges surprise.
easy.explanation: p-values are computed under the null; they are not posterior probabilities of H₀.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Assume H₀: μ = 100, SE = 2, and observe x̄ = 105 (z = 2.5). Step 2: p = P(|Z| ≥ 2.5) ≈ 0.012 — rarity under H₀. Step 3: It never states P(H₀ true); H₀ has no probability in this framework. Step 4: Small p means the data surprise H₀, nothing more.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That would be a Bayesian posterior, not a frequentist p-value.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: α is a chosen threshold; p is computed from data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: p-values don't directly give P(Hₐ false).

easy.prompt: A p-value of 0.03 at α = 0.05 means…
easy.hint: Next step: compare p with α — smaller p clears the bar.
easy.explanation: p < α ⇒ reject H₀ in the standard fixed-α framework.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: α = 0.05 draws the rejection line. Step 2: p = 0.03 falls past it (0.03 < 0.05). Step 3: Such extreme data occur only 3% of the time under H₀. Step 4: So H₀'s story is rejected at 5% — while 0.03 never measured P(H₀ true).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 0.03 < 0.05 leads to rejection, not retention.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: p is not P(H₀ true).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: We never 'accept' H₀; we fail to reject or reject.

easy.prompt: Rejecting a true null hypothesis is called…
easy.hint: Next step: match 'reject' + 'true H₀' — a false alarm.
easy.explanation: Type I = false positive (reject true H₀); controlled by α.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: H₀ true (drug = placebo) but the trial rejects. Step 2: That's a false alarm: Type I. Step 3: At α = 0.05 it happens ~5% of true-null trials. Step 4: Type II is the opposite miss (keeping a false H₀).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Type II is failing to reject a false H₀.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Power is 1 − P(Type II), not Type I.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Confidence applies to intervals, not this error label.

easy.prompt: Statistical power is…

choices.label: B
choices.body: P(correctly reject H₀ | a stated alternative is true)

easy.hint: Next step: condition on the effect being real — power is the detection rate.
easy.explanation: Power = 1 − β: how often the test catches a specified real effect.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: True effect d = 0.5, n = 64 per group: power ≈ 0.80. Step 2: Run 100 such studies: ~80 reject. Step 3: P(reject | H₀ true) is α = 0.05 instead — a different conditional. Step 4: Power varies by design; 0.80 is convention, not law.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's α (Type I rate), conditioning on H₀.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Frequentist power assigns H₀ no probability.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Power ranges 0-1 with n, effect, and α.

easy.prompt: A chi-square test is used when data are…
easy.hint: Next step: check the data type — chi-square eats contingency tables, not raw means.
easy.explanation: χ² compares observed counts to expected counts under H₀.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: 200 voters × {Yes, No, Undecided}: counts (90, 70, 40). Step 2: Under equal split, expect (66.7, 66.7, 66.7). Step 3: χ² = Σ(O−E)²/E ≈ 19.0. Step 4: Means-based t/ANOVA would mishandle these categories.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Continuous means call for t/ANOVA/z.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Paired differences call for paired t.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: One proportion uses z; χ² handles whole tables.

easy.prompt: ANOVA is used to compare…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Means across three or more groups

easy.hint: Next step: count the groups — three-plus means call for ANOVA.
easy.explanation: One F-test asks whether any group mean differs, controlling overall error.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Diets A, B, C: x̄ = (4, 6, 9) lb lost. Step 2: Three t-tests would triple-dip error. Step 3: ANOVA's single F pools all data first. Step 4: Two groups only? A t-test suffices.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Proportions across groups use χ².
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Two means are t-test territory; ANOVA generalizes upward.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Correlation is regression's job.

easy.prompt: In a significance test, the null hypothesis H₀ is…

choices.label: B
choices.body: The default claim tested for possible rejection

easy.hint: Next step: think status quo — H₀ is the skeptic's position data must overcome.
easy.explanation: We assume H₀ unless data provide strong enough evidence against it.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: H₀: μ = 100 (no effect). Step 2: Data x̄ = 105, SE = 2 → z = 2.5, p ≈ 0.012. Step 3: Evidence clears α = 0.05, so H₀ falls. Step 4: Without such evidence H₀ stands — never 'proven', just retained.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: H₀ is often no-effect, against the researcher's wish.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: p measures evidence against H₀; it isn't H₀.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Hypotheses are statements, not probabilities here.

easy.prompt: A result with p = 0.30 (α = 0.05) means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The effect is proven to be exactly zero

choices.label: B
choices.body: No significant evidence: the effect could be zero or too small to detect here

easy.hint: Next step: separate 'not significant' from 'no effect' — ask about power.
easy.explanation: Non-significance reflects evidence strength, not effect size; small studies miss real effects.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: n = 20, true d = 0.3: power ≈ 0.20 — misses 80% of the time. Step 2: p = 0.30 is the typical outcome then. Step 3: The 95% CI might span (−0.2, +0.8) — includes 0 AND large effects. Step 4: 'No evidence' ≠ 'evidence of none'.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: CIs still admit sizable effects; zero is just one survivor.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: H₀ is never proven by big p.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: p = 0.30 with n = 20 smells underpowered, not perfect.

easy.prompt: You run 20 independent tests, all nulls true, at α = 0.05. Expected false rejections?
easy.hint: Next step: multiply tests by per-test error rate.
easy.explanation: Expected Type I errors ≈ m·α = 20×0.05 = 1.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Each true-null test falsely rejects w.p. 0.05. Step 2: Linearity of expectation: 20 × 0.05 = 1. Step 3: P(≥1 false) is higher still: 1 − 0.95^20 ≈ 0.64. Step 4: So one 'hit' among 20 is the null-world default, not a discovery.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's α per test, not the 20-test total.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That needs every test to reject — absurd under true nulls.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Not m·α for m = 20.

easy.prompt: For least-squares regression, slope b₁ = r·(sy/sx). If r = 0.8, sx = 5, sy = 10, what is b₁?
easy.hint: Next step: plug into r times (sy over sx).
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Ratio sy/sx = 10/5 = 2. Step 2: Multiply by r: 0.8 × 2 = 1.6. Step 3: Each extra x-unit predicts +1.6 y-units. Step 4: Inverting the ratio (0.4) would shrink instead of stretch.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That inverts the ratio (sx/sy).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That doubles incorrectly (r·sy/sx needs /5, giving 1.6).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's r·sy, missing the /sx scaling.

easy.prompt: In regression, the least-squares line always passes through which point?
easy.hint: Next step: recall the intercept formula b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄ — plug x̄ in.
easy.explanation: The fitted line satisfies ȳ = b₀ + b₁x̄, so it goes through the sample means.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄ by construction. Step 2: Predict at x̄: b₀ + b₁x̄ = ȳ. Step 3: With x̄ = 10, ȳ = 20, b₁ = 1.6: line gives 4 + 16 = 20. ✓ Step 4: Corners like (min x, min y) have no such guarantee.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Only if both means are zero.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The line need not touch data-cloud corners.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Extremes need not lie on the LS line.

easy.prompt: The correlation coefficient r always lies between…
easy.hint: Next step: recall standardization — r is a mean of z-products, bounded by alignment.
easy.explanation: r measures linear association strength and direction on a bounded scale.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Perfect uphill line: z-products average +1. Step 2: Perfect downhill: −1. Step 3: Cloud with no tilt: ~0. Step 4: No arrangement escapes [−1, 1] (Cauchy-Schwarz).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Negative associations produce negative r.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: r is standardized and bounded.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Percent scales aren't used for r.

easy.prompt: A residual for one observation equals…

choices.label: C
choices.body: x minus the mean of x

easy.hint: Next step: sign it as reality minus model — leftovers after prediction.
easy.explanation: Residuals are what the line failed to explain, signed by direction.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: y = 90, ŷ = 84: residual +6 (under-predicted). Step 2: y = 78, ŷ = 84: residual −6. Step 3: Sum of LS residuals ≈ 0 by construction. Step 4: Plotting them against x exposes missed curvature.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Sign follows y − ŷ; over-predictions go negative.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's a deviation of x, not a prediction error.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Slope×x is a fitted component, not the leftover.

easy.prompt: A model fit on ages 5-12 predicts reading score from age. Predicting for age 30 is…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Extrapolation: risky, since the age-score relationship changes beyond childhood

easy.hint: Next step: check the data's range — 30 sits far outside 5-12.
easy.explanation: Relationships estimated in-range can break out-of-range (plateaus, new regimes).
easy.deepDive: Step 1: In-range: +8 points/year, R² = 0.9. Step 2: Extend to 30: predicts 5-12 line +18×8 = +144 over age 12 — absurd. Step 3: Real reading plateaus ~age 15. Step 4: High in-sample R² never licenses far extrapolation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Lines extend mathematically, not empirically.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Interpolation stays inside 5-12; 30 is outside.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: R² describes the fitting window only.

easy.prompt: Ice-cream sales and drownings correlate strongly. Best conclusion?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Confounding (summer heat) drives both; correlation ≠ causation

easy.hint: Next step: hunt the third variable — what season brings both?
easy.explanation: A lurking variable (temperature/season) explains the association without direct causation.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: July: sales $50k, 30 drownings; January: $5k, 2 drownings. Step 2: Within-July days, sales vs drownings r ≈ 0 — association vanishes. Step 3: Temperature predicts both: hot → swimmers + buyers. Step 4: Banning ice cream would save no swimmers.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: No mechanism; the confounder explains all.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Reverse causation is equally unevidenced.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Correlations flag candidates — then design decides.

easy.prompt: In multiple regression, a coefficient is read as the effect…
easy.hint: Next step: add the ceteris-paribus clause — 'other things equal'.
easy.explanation: Multiple regression adjusts: each slope is the residual effect after the rest.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Score ~ hours + GPA: b_hours = 2. Step 2: Among students with GPA 3.0, +1 hour → +2 points. Step 3: Simple regression (no GPA) gave 3.5 — GPA confounded it. Step 4: 'Holding fixed' is the adjustment payoff.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's simple regression's marginal reading.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Coefficients never sum across predictors.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Intercept is the all-x-zero prediction, a separate piece.

easy.prompt: Logistic regression is used when the outcome is…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Binary (0/1): it models P(y = 1) through an S-curve

easy.hint: Next step: match model to outcome — binary needs probabilities in [0,1].
easy.explanation: Logit link squeezes linear scores into valid probabilities.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Pass/fail vs hours: linear score −4 + 1.2×hours. Step 2: At 5h: score 2.0 → p = 1/(1+e^−2) ≈ 0.88. Step 3: At 1h: score −2.8 → p ≈ 0.057. Step 4: S-curve respects both floor and ceiling.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Continuous y uses ordinary linear regression.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Counts use Poisson, not logistic.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Binary outcomes are Bernoulli, never normal.

easy.prompt: An INFLUENTIAL point in regression is one that…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Combines leverage (extreme x) with discrepancy so removing it shifts the fit notably

easy.hint: Next step: need both ingredients — far x AND off-line y.
easy.explanation: Leverage × discrepancy = influence; either alone may be harmless.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Point at x = 50 (rest ≤ 10) on the line: high leverage, no influence. Step 2: Point at x = 5 with huge residual: outlier, low leverage, mild influence. Step 3: Point at x = 50 far off-line: slope swings 1.6 → 0.4 on removal. Step 4: That third kind rules the fit.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Large residuals at central x barely tilt the line.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: On-line points reinforce the fit, never distort it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Average x means minimal leverage.

medium.prompt: A machine fills bottles to a target of 500 mL with small random errors, giving mean 500.1 mL and median 500.0 mL. What shape is most plausible?
medium.hint: Next step: check how close mean and median are — near-equal means balanced tails.
medium.explanation: Mean essentially equals median, so errors balance on both sides with no long tail.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: The gap is only 0.1 mL, under 0.1% of a typical 2-3 mL fill SD. Step 2: Random over- and under-fills cancel in the average. Step 3: With 200 bottles the SE of the mean is only about 0.2 mL, so a 0.1 gap is pure noise. Step 4: Near-equal center measures with one central mound means approximately symmetric.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Right skew would push the mean clearly above the median, not 0.1 mL apart.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Left skew would pull the mean clearly below the median.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Two machines would show two humps in the histogram, not one mound.

medium.prompt: A dataset has mean 100 and median 80. Which statement is most plausible?

choices.label: B
choices.body: The distribution is right-skewed with large high outliers

choices.label: C
choices.body: The distribution is left-skewed with low outliers

choices.label: D
choices.body: Mean and median must match for any data

medium.hint: Next step: follow the mean — it leans toward the tail, and here it leans high.
medium.explanation: Mean clearly above median is the classic fingerprint of a right tail pulling the average up.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: The 20-point gap exceeds what sampling noise explains at ordinary sample sizes. Step 2: Suppose 90 values near 75 plus 10 values near 325: the median stays near 75-80. Step 3: The mean becomes (90(75) + 10(325))/100 = 100 exactly. Step 4: A few large values manufacture the whole gap, confirming right skew.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Symmetric data would put mean and median within noise of each other.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Low outliers would drag the mean below the median, the opposite pattern.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Skew routinely separates mean and median; equality holds mainly under symmetry.

medium.prompt: Which statement about variance and standard deviation is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Variance can be negative for skewed data

choices.label: B
choices.body: Variance is in squared units; SD restores original units

choices.label: C
choices.body: SD is always larger than the range

choices.label: D
choices.body: SD equals the IQR in every dataset

medium.hint: Next step: track the units — squaring deviations squares the units too.
medium.explanation: Variance averages squared deviations (squared units); its square root returns to data units.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: For heights with SD 6 cm, variance is 36 cm². Step 2: Square-centimeters cannot be plotted on a height axis directly. Step 3: Taking √36 cm² = 6 cm restores comparability with the mean. Step 4: That is why reports quote SD, not variance, beside the mean.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Variance sums squares, so it can never go negative.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SD is often far smaller than the range; e.g., SD 6 cm with range 30 cm.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: SD and IQR coincide only in special cases, not by definition.

medium.prompt: Which spread measure resists outliers: range, standard deviation, or IQR?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Standard deviation, because it averages everything

choices.label: C
choices.body: IQR, because it uses only the middle 50%

medium.hint: Next step: ask which values each formula touches — measures touching extremes inherit them.
medium.explanation: The IQR trims the outer quarters, so extremes never enter the calculation.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Add a $1M income to nine $50k incomes: range explodes from $0 to $950k. Step 2: SD jumps from 0 to about $287k. Step 3: Q1 and Q3 stay at $50k, so IQR stays $0. Step 4: Only the IQR ignored the intruder, proving its resistance.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Range is defined by the two most extreme points, so one outlier rewrites it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: SD squares every deviation, so a far outlier dominates the average.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The example shows range and SD moved enormously while IQR sat still.

medium.prompt: Data: 3, 3, 5, 7, 7, 7, 9. Using lower half {3,3,5} and upper half {7,7,7,9}, what are Q1 and Q3?
medium.hint: Next step: split at the median 7, then take the median of each half.
medium.explanation: Lower-half median is 3 and upper-half median is 7, giving IQR 4.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Ordered data 3,3,5,7,7,7,9 have overall median 7 (4th of 7). Step 2: Lower half {3,3,5} has middle value 3, so Q1 = 3. Step 3: Upper half {7,7,7,9} (values above the median position) has middle between 7 and 7, i.e., 7. Step 4: IQR = 7 − 3 = 4.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 5 is the lower-half max and 9 the overall max, not half-medians.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Averaging endpoints is not the quartile rule used here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 9 is the maximum; Q3 is the upper-half median 7.

medium.prompt: Two boxplots: Group X median 50 with box 40-60; Group Y median 65 with box 55-75. Which comparison is sound?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Y's typical value exceeds X's; boxes overlap only slightly

choices.label: C
choices.body: X varies more because its median is lower

choices.label: D
choices.body: Boxplots prove Y causes higher values

medium.hint: Next step: compare the inside lines for center, then box overlap for separation.
medium.explanation: The median lines differ by 15 and the boxes barely overlap, so Y runs typically higher.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Median gap is 65 − 50 = 15 units. Step 2: X's box tops at 60 while Y's box starts at 55, overlapping only on 55-60. Step 3: So over 75% of Y exceeds X's median region. Step 4: That is a real distributional shift, though not proof of causation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The inside lines sit at 50 vs 65, clearly different.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Box widths (both 20) match, so variation is similar; median height is not spread.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Boxplots show association, never causation by themselves.

medium.prompt: With Q1 = 30 and Q3 = 50, values below what threshold are flagged as low outliers?
medium.hint: Next step: mirror the fence downward — subtract 1.5 IQRs from Q1.
medium.explanation: IQR is 20, so the low fence is 30 − 1.5(20) = 0.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: IQR = 50 − 30 = 20. Step 2: Reach is 1.5 × 20 = 30. Step 3: Subtract from Q1: 30 − 30 = 0. Step 4: Values below 0 (e.g., −5) flag as low outliers.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 20 subtracts only 0.5 IQR from Q1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 15 subtracts only 0.75 IQR from Q1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 30 is Q1 itself, the 25th percentile, not a fence.

medium.prompt: Exam A: mean 70, SD 5; Exam B: mean 80, SD 10. Ana scores 75 on A and 85 on B. On which did she do relatively better?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Equally, both 5 points above the mean

choices.label: D
choices.body: Exam B, because larger SD means better

medium.hint: Next step: standardize each score — divide the raw gap by that exam's SD.
medium.explanation: z_A = (75−70)/5 = 1.0 exceeds z_B = (85−80)/10 = 0.5, so A is the stronger relative performance.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Raw gaps are both 5 points. Step 2: On A, 5 points equal one full SD (5/5 = 1.0). Step 3: On B, 5 points equal half an SD (5/10 = 0.5). Step 4: Percentile-wise z = 1.0 (~84th) beats z = 0.5 (~69th).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Raw points ignore the exams' different scales and spreads.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Equal raw gaps give unequal z when SDs differ (5/5 vs 5/10).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Larger SD shrinks z for the same gap — it hurts relative standing, not helps.

medium.prompt: Batter A hits better than B in the first half (.300 vs .280) and in the second half (.250 vs .240), but B's full-season average is higher. What explains it?

choices.label: A
choices.body: B had more at-bats in the half where averages were higher

medium.hint: Next step: weight each half by at-bats — a half with many at-bats dominates the season line.
medium.explanation: Unequal at-bats across halves weight the halves differently, letting B's hot half count more.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: A: 100 AB at .300 (30 H) + 300 AB at .250 (75 H) = 105/400 = .2625. Step 2: B: 300 AB at .280 (84 H) + 100 AB at .240 (24 H) = 108/400 = .270. Step 3: B loses each half yet banks 84 hits in the high-average half versus A's 30. Step 4: Season average is AB-weighted, so volume in the easier half wins.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No cheating is needed; weighting alone produces the reversal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Season average is total hits over total at-bats by definition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The splits reveal the weighting mechanism behind the paradox.

medium.prompt: A university's overall admission rate is higher for men, but within each department women are admitted at equal or higher rates. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Discrimination proven by the overall rate

choices.label: B
choices.body: Women applied disproportionately to selective departments

choices.label: D
choices.body: Overall rates are the only fair comparison

medium.hint: Next step: compare application destinations — tougher departments drag down whoever applies there most.
medium.explanation: Self-selection into competitive departments depresses the pooled rate for women despite fair within-department rates.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Suppose Physics admits 20% and History 80%. Step 2: 80 women apply to Physics (16 admitted) and 20 to History (16 admitted): pooled 32/100 = 32%. Step 3: 20 men apply to Physics (4 admitted) and 80 to History (64 admitted): pooled 68/100 = 68%. Step 4: Within each department rates are equal, yet pooled rates differ wildly — the classic Berkeley-style reversal.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The overall gap reflects application mix, and within-department parity contradicts that verdict.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Real Berkeley 1973 data show exactly this pattern without fabrication.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Stratified comparisons control the confounder; the pooled rate ignores it.

medium.prompt: Why do histograms use contiguous (touching) bars while categorical bar charts leave gaps?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Histograms track a numeric scale where bins adjoin; gaps would falsely split the continuum

choices.label: C
choices.body: Categorical charts also require touching bars

medium.hint: Next step: ask what the x-axis is — numbers flow continuously, categories do not.
medium.explanation: Histogram bins partition a number line with no holes, so bars touch; categories are separate, so bars stand apart.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Bins 0-10, 10-20, 20-30 tile the axis edge to edge. Step 2: A gap would imply no values exist there, which is false. Step 3: Categories like Red/Blue have no between-values, so gaps correctly signal separateness. Step 4: Touch vs gap thus encodes continuous vs discrete axes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Adjoining bins are meaningful: each shared edge is a real cut point like 10.0.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Standard categorical charts separate bars to show unrelated groups.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Bar height/area in a histogram is exactly the bin frequency or proportion.

medium.prompt: A dataset of 500 exam scores looks like noise with 60 tiny bins but a clear mound with 12 wider bins. What happened?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Wider bins removed all outliers illegally

choices.label: B
choices.body: Tiny bins undersmooth: sampling noise swamps shape; wider bins reveal it

choices.label: D
choices.body: 500 scores are too few for any histogram

medium.prompt: Which statement about the streak HHHHHH is correct?

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's P(no heads), the complement of the target.

medium.prompt: A and B are disjoint with P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.3. Can they be independent?

choices.label: A

medium.hint: Next step: test the product rule — independence demands joint = product.
medium.explanation: Disjoint forces P(A∩B) = 0, but independence needs 0.4×0.3 = 0.12 — contradiction.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Disjoint means no shared outcomes: joint = 0. Step 2: Independent would need joint = 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.12. Step 3: 0 ≠ 0.12, so both cannot hold. Step 4: Learning A occurred kills B entirely — maximal dependence, not independence.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Disjointness (exclusion) fights independence (irrelevance) when probs are positive.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Sums below 1 say nothing about the product rule.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Marginals plus disjointness fully determine the joint (0), so we can tell.

medium.prompt: Independent events A, B each have positive probability. Can they ALSO be disjoint?

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Summing to 1 is about unions, and still leaves joint at product > 0.

medium.prompt: Sample means from n = 100 independent observations with finite variance are approximately normal because of…

medium.prompt: Which sampling distribution is closest to normal: means of n = 4, n = 30, or n = 200 from an exponential population?

medium.prompt: Why do textbooks say 'n ≥ 30' for CLT use?

medium.prompt: A sample of 500 river mercury readings is serially correlated (nearby readings alike). What is the concern?

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No ban exists; z approximates t once n is large.
