wrongAnswerExplanations.c: An interval straddling 0 argues against claiming a large effect.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Wide-but-valid intervals are inconclusive, not invalid.

medium.prompt: 30 dieters: mean loss d̄ = 4 lb, sd of losses = 6 lb. The 95% CI for mean loss is…
medium.hint: Next step: SE = 6/√30, then × t* ≈ 2.045.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: √30 ≈ 5.477; SE = 6/5.477 ≈ 1.0954. Step 2: df = 29, t* ≈ 2.045; margin ≈ 2.240. Step 3: (4−2.24, 4+2.24) = (1.76, 6.24). Step 4: Zero excluded → significant mean loss at 5%.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That spans a full SD — ~5.5× the real margin.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's ±1 SE (≈68%), half the needed multiplier.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 10 sums d̄ with sd — meaningless center.

medium.prompt: When should you NOT pair?

choices.label: A
choices.body: When pairs are naturally linked (twins, before/after)

choices.label: B
choices.body: When samples are independent with no natural pairing — forced pairing wastes df

medium.hint: Next step: ask if a real link exists — pairing arbitrary strangers manufactures nothing.
medium.explanation: Artificial pairs add no variance removal and cost degrees of freedom.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Pairing 20 men with 20 unrelated women: differences still carry full person-variance. Step 2: df drops from ~38 to 19, widening t* from 2.02 to 2.09. Step 3: Same SE, bigger multiplier → wider CI, pure loss. Step 4: Pair only on genuine links (same subject, matched twins).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's exactly when pairing shines.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Large n doesn't forbid pairing; absent links do.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Normal differences are ideal for pairing, not a veto.

medium.prompt: n = 10 heavily right-skewed turnaround times. Why does the t-interval misbehave?

choices.label: B
choices.body: x̄'s distribution is still right-skewed: misses land asymmetrically and coverage drops

choices.label: D
choices.body: Small samples are always exactly normal

medium.hint: Next step: picture x̄ over reruns — with n = 10 the skew survives averaging.
medium.explanation: Upper misses exceed lower misses; actual coverage can sink to ~85% for nominal 95%.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Population skew ≈ 3; x̄ skew ≈ 3/√10 ≈ 0.95 — still large. Step 2: Symmetric t criticals can't match the lopsided x̄. Step 3: Simulation: ~10% upper misses + ~5% lower vs 2.5/2.5 intended. Step 4: Log-scale or median intervals behave better here.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 30 is guidance; 10 fails because of skew, not a magic cutoff.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Skew distorts means first — that is the whole problem.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Small samples inherit population shape; normality needs earning.

medium.prompt: Method A: 95% CI width 10 with true 95% coverage. Method B: width 6 but only 80% coverage. Which is 'better' at 95% nominal?

choices.label: B
choices.body: A — B's narrowness comes from breaking its 95% promise

medium.hint: Next step: compare like with like — width is only fair at equal coverage.
medium.explanation: 15 points of missing coverage disqualify B at the 95% nominal level.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: In 100 reruns A misses ~5, B misses ~20. Step 2: B's 6-width looks sharp but lies about its confidence. Step 3: Widened to honest 95%, B would span ~9-10 too. Step 4: Judge precision only among methods that keep their coverage promise.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Narrower wins only with coverage held equal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A keeps its advertised error rate; B quadruples it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Width matters — after coverage is secured.

medium.prompt: A test gives p = 0.40. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.label: B
choices.body: No significant evidence against H₀; H₀ stays unrejected (effect may still exist)

choices.label: D
choices.body: The effect size must be zero

medium.hint: Next step: ask what big p says — 'not surprising under H₀', not 'H₀ confirmed'.
medium.explanation: Large p means the data fit H₀ well enough; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: p = 0.40: 40% of H₀-world reruns look this extreme — utterly ordinary. Step 2: So we fail to reject. Step 3: But a real effect of, say, d = 0.2 with n = 20 also yields p ≈ 0.40 often (low power). Step 4: Non-rejection coexists with real effects the study was too small to see.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Tests never prove H₀; they only fail to reject it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: p = 0.40 is far from the rejection region.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Effect could be nonzero but undetected — CIs would show the range.

medium.prompt: Failing to reject H₀ when the alternative is actually true is…
medium.hint: Next step: match 'missed detection' — the alarm that never rang.
medium.explanation: Type II = false negative; its rate β falls as power rises.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Drug truly works, but the small trial's p = 0.20 keeps H₀. Step 2: The real effect slipped through — Type II. Step 3: If power is 0.80, this happens 20% of the time. Step 4: 'Proof of H₀' is never on the menu.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Type I needs a rejection of a true H₀ — neither happened.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Non-rejection never proves H₀.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Missing effects is the opposite of gaining significance.

medium.prompt: A test has power 0.80 against a specific alternative. If H₀ is false in that way, P(correctly reject H₀) is…
medium.hint: Next step: read power's definition — detection rate when the effect is real.
medium.explanation: Power = 1 − β = P(reject H₀ | Hₐ true in the stated way).
medium.deepDive: Step 1: β = 0.20 is the miss rate under this alternative. Step 2: 1 − 0.20 = 0.80 detect. Step 3: Over 100 such trials, ~80 reject, ~20 miss. Step 4: 0.05 would be the false-alarm rate under H₀ — a different world.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's β (Type II rate), the complement of power.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's a common α, the H₀-world error rate.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Power below 1 leaves a real miss chance.

medium.prompt: Which change INCREASES power (same α)?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Larger true effect or larger n

medium.hint: Next step: ask what separates signal from noise — bigger signal, more data, less noise.
medium.explanation: Power rises with effect size and n, and falls with noise.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Effect 0.5σ at n = 25/group: power ≈ 0.41. Step 2: Same effect at n = 64: power ≈ 0.80. Step 3: Double the effect at n = 25: power ≈ 0.80 too. Step 4: Extra noise (bigger σ) reverses all these gains.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Less data means a noisier x̄ and fewer detections.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Noise buries the signal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Two-sided splits α and slightly costs power vs one-sided.

medium.prompt: Study A (n = 30) finds p = 0.20 for a real effect d = 0.3; Study B tests the same effect with n = 300 and rejects. What explains it?

choices.label: B
choices.body: A lacked power (~0.28): non-significance reflected imprecision, not absence

medium.hint: Next step: compute SE in each — same effect, very different noise.
medium.explanation: SE_A ≈ σ/√30 vs SE_B ≈ σ/√300 (3.16× tighter); B can see what A can't.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: z_A ≈ 0.3·√30/2 ≈ 0.82 → p ≈ 0.41-ish (two-sample scaling aside, clearly weak). Step 2: Power_A ≈ 0.28: misses ~72% of the time. Step 3: Power_B ≈ 0.99 with 10× the data. Step 4: A's p = 0.20 is exactly what an underpowered real effect looks like.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Underpowered non-rejection never disproves.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Bigger-n significance is expected, not suspicious per se.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: p-values depend on n through SE — strongly.

medium.prompt: A goodness-of-fit test has 4 categories. Its degrees of freedom are…
medium.hint: Next step: one constraint (total n fixed) removes one degree.
medium.explanation: df = categories − 1 = 3.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: 4 free counts would be 4 df. Step 2: They must sum to n = 200 — one linear constraint. Step 3: 4 − 1 = 3. Step 4: χ² = 9.2 on df 3 gives p ≈ 0.027 — reject equal shares at 5%.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Forgets the sum-to-n constraint.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 16 is 4² — no squaring in df.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 1 df fits 2×2 independence, not 4-category fit.

medium.prompt: ANOVA gives F = 8.2 with p = 0.001 for 3 fertilizers. What does this mean?

choices.label: A
choices.body: All three means are proven equal

choices.label: B
choices.body: Between-group variation dwarfs within-group noise; at least one mean differs

medium.hint: Next step: read F as signal-over-noise — big F means real separation.
medium.explanation: F = MS_between/MS_within; 8.2 with p = 0.001 rejects all-equal.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Within-field SD ≈ 2 (noise). Step 2: Group means spread ≈ ±4 (signal). Step 3: Variance ratio 8.2 occurs ~1 rerun in 1000 under all-equal. Step 4: Follow with post-hoc tests to find WHICH pairs differ.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: p = 0.001 rejects equality, the reverse.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 8.2 is a variance ratio, not a mean gap.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: ANOVA doesn't crown winners — post-hocs do.

medium.prompt: A two-sided z-test of H₀: μ = 100 vs Hₐ: μ ≠ 100 at α = 0.05 rejects when |z| exceeds…
medium.hint: Next step: split α into both tails — 2.5% each side.
medium.explanation: Two-sided 5% critical values are ±1.96.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Standard normal: middle 95% spans ±1.96. Step 2: |z| = 2.1 → reject (p ≈ 0.036). Step 3: |z| = 1.5 → keep (p ≈ 0.134). Step 4: 1.645 is the one-sided 5% line; 2.58 is two-sided 1%.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's the one-sided 5% cutoff.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's two-sided 1%.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's α, not a z value.

medium.prompt: A 95% CI for μ lies entirely above 0. For H₀: μ = 0 vs Hₐ: μ ≠ 0 at α = 0.05, you should…

choices.label: D
choices.body: Conclude μ equals the upper endpoint

medium.hint: Next step: apply duality — outside the interval means rejected at the matching level.
medium.explanation: Interval excludes 0 ⇔ two-sided test rejects μ = 0 at 5%.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: CI (2, 8): every plausible μ is positive. Step 2: 0 is implausible at 95% confidence. Step 3: Equivalently z = x̄/SE ≈ 5/1.5 ≈ 3.3, p ≈ 0.001. Step 4: Same data, same verdict — estimation and testing agree.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 0 outside the CI is inconsistent with H₀.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Tests don't yield P(H₀ true).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The CI bounds a range; no endpoint is the verdict.

medium.prompt: With n = 100,000, a 0.1-point IQ gap (p < 0.001) is found. How should you read it?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Hugely important because p is tiny

choices.label: B
choices.body: Statistically significant but practically trivial — report the effect size

medium.hint: Next step: look past p at the number — 0.1 points changes nothing in life.
medium.explanation: Enormous n detects microscopic gaps; significance ≠ importance.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: SE ≈ 15/√100000 ≈ 0.047; z ≈ 0.1/0.047 ≈ 2.1+… (scales to p < 0.001 with full n per group). Step 2: CI ≈ (0.05, 0.15) — precisely tiny. Step 3: A 0.1-point gap is ~1/150 of a SD: invisible individually. Step 4: Lead with '0.1 points (95% CI …)', not the stars.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Tiny p here certifies precision, not bigness.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Large n is valid — it just answers a sharper question than asked.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Observational gaps never prove causation alone.

medium.prompt: p = 0.06 at α = 0.05. The correct statement is…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Not significant at 5%: fail to reject (report p and the CI, not 'almost')

medium.hint: Next step: hold the line — the rule was fixed before data arrived.
medium.explanation: 0.06 > 0.05 keeps H₀; 'marginal significance' is spin, not a verdict.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: The 5% line was pre-registered. Step 2: 0.06 misses it — like missing a train by a minute. Step 3: Report p = 0.06 plus CI, e.g., (−0.1, 4.3), showing what remains plausible. Step 4: p says nothing about size — only compatibility with H₀.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Rounding the p-value to cross the line is cheating.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: H₀ has no probability here, barely or otherwise.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Size needs an estimate (d, CI) — p can't supply it.

medium.prompt: With 20 tests, the Bonferroni-corrected per-test level for overall 5% is…
medium.hint: Next step: split α across tests — 0.05/20.
medium.explanation: Bonferroni: α* = 0.05/20 = 0.0025 per test.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Union bound: P(any false) ≤ Σ P(false_i) = 20α*. Step 2: Set 20α* = 0.05 → α* = 0.0025. Step 3: Only p < 0.0025 counts per test. Step 4: Conservative (power costs) but valid under any dependence.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Uncorrected 0.05 gives ~64% family-wise error over 20 tests.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 0.50 per test guarantees floods of false alarms.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 0.95 is a confidence level, not a per-test α.

medium.prompt: Regression line ŷ = 2 + 1.6x was fit on study hours (x) vs score gain (y). Predict the gain for x = 10 hours.
medium.hint: Next step: substitute x = 10 into the equation.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Slope contribution: 1.6 × 10 = 16. Step 2: Add intercept: 2 + 16 = 18. Step 3: So 10 hours predicts +18 points. Step 4: This is estimation of the mean gain, not a promise for any individual.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's 1.6 + 2 — adding instead of multiplying by 10.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's the per-hour rate, not the 10-hour prediction.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That multiplies intercept too: (2+1.6)×10 — wrong order.

medium.prompt: R² = 0.64 in simple linear regression means…

choices.label: B
choices.body: 64% of y's variation is explained by the linear model

medium.hint: Next step: read R² as a fraction — explained variance over total variance.
medium.explanation: R² is the squared correlation in simple regression: fraction of variance explained.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Total variance of y: say 100 units. Step 2: Model accounts for 64; residuals keep 36. Step 3: r = ±0.8 (sign from slope) since 0.8² = 0.64. Step 4: 36% remains — prediction still errs substantially.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: r is ±0.8 (r² = 0.64), sign matching the slope.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Residuals are rarely zero; R² measures explained variation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: R² is not the slope.

medium.prompt: Study hours (x) vs exam score (y) show positive correlation. What does that mean?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Higher x tends to occur with higher y

choices.label: C
choices.body: Higher x tends to occur with lower y

medium.hint: Next step: translate sign to tilt — positive means uphill cloud.
medium.explanation: Positive r: upward trend; causation needs design, not correlation alone.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: r = +0.6: 10-hour studiers average ~75, 2-hour studiers ~60. Step 2: Scatter still overlaps — some light studiers ace it. Step 3: Motivation could drive both (confounding). Step 4: Uphill ≠ proven causal.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Correlation never establishes causation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That describes negative correlation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Positive correlation IS an upward linear pattern.

medium.prompt: A residual plot shows a clear curved (smile) pattern while r = 0.9. Best conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The linear model is perfect because r is large

choices.label: B
choices.body: Linear model inadequate despite high r; consider transformation or nonlinear terms

medium.hint: Next step: trust the plot over the number — systematic curves mean missed structure.
medium.explanation: r measures linear association; systematic curvature violates linearity.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Residuals run −5, −1, +3, −1, −5 across x: a U, not noise. Step 2: r = 0.9 reflects the overall rise, blind to the bend. Step 3: Adding x² (quadratic) flattens residuals and lifts R² 0.81 → 0.97. Step 4: High r with curved residuals is the classic fool's comfort.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: High r coexists with systematic curvature.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Outliers and curvature can coexist.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: r can be high for monotone nonlinear patterns too.

medium.prompt: A good residual plot for linear regression looks like…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A clear funnel widening to the right

choices.label: B
choices.body: A formless cloud centered at zero with steady vertical spread

medium.hint: Next step: want no pattern — leftover noise should look like noise.
medium.explanation: Random scatter around zero supports linearity, constant variance, and (roughly) normality.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Residuals between −8 and +8 at all x: steady band. Step 2: Mean ≈ 0 at left, middle, right — no tilt left. Step 3: No funnel, no curve. Step 4: Funnel/U/line each diagnose a specific violation instead.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Funnel = heteroscedasticity (non-constant variance).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Points ON a line means y is deterministic in x — no real data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: U-shape = missed curvature.

medium.prompt: House-price model fit on 800-2000 sq ft predicts a 8000 sq ft mansion's price. Main danger?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Extrapolation: luxury segment follows different pricing (land, prestige) unobserved in-range

medium.hint: Next step: ask what 8000 sq ft estates add — features absent from small homes.
medium.explanation: Out-of-range predictions assume the in-range slope persists into a new market regime.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: In-range slope: +$150/sq ft. Step 2: Naive: 8000×150 = $1.2M + base. Step 3: Actual mansions: land scarcity and prestige add nonlinear premia — errors of 50%+ typical. Step 4: Honest answer: report 'outside data range', refit with luxury comps.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 8000 is far outside 800-2000 — extrapolation, not interpolation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No R² requirement exists for validity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Math allows it; evidence doesn't support it.

medium.prompt: Sleep-deprived students get lower grades (r = −0.5). Can we claim less sleep causes lower grades?

choices.label: B
choices.body: No — confounders (stress, study habits, health) and reverse causation are open; need experiments

choices.label: D
choices.body: No, negative correlations can't be causal

medium.hint: Next step: list rival stories — could grades (stress) cut sleep instead?
medium.explanation: Observational correlation admits multiple causal graphs; size doesn't arbitrate.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Anxious students sleep 5h and score 70; calm ones sleep 8h and score 85. Step 2: Anxiety → less sleep AND lower scores explains r = −0.5 fully. Step 3: Or failing grades cause worry that cuts sleep (reverse arrow). Step 4: Randomize sleep (ethically tricky) or adjust richly before causal talk.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: No observational number proves causation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: |−0.5| is moderate — and magnitude never settles direction.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Negative effects are causal all the time (toxins); sign is irrelevant.

medium.prompt: Adding pure-noise predictors to a regression will, across many samples, tend to…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Not improve true prediction; in-sample R² never falls (overfitting)

medium.hint: Next step: ask if R² can drop when new coefficients may sit at zero.
medium.explanation: The optimizer keeps or improves sample fit; out-of-sample noise hurts.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Base R² = 0.40. Step 2: Add random z: fit climbs to 0.43 (fits noise quirks). Step 3: Test-set MSE worsens 100 → 108. Step 4: Adjusted R²/AIC expose the fake gain.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: R² never decreases adding predictors, in-sample.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Noise variables are usually insignificant.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Perfect fit needs ~n predictors, not one noise column.

medium.prompt: Two predictors correlate at r = 0.95. Each is insignificant alone in the model, but the pair is jointly strong. Diagnosis?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Multicollinearity: redundant info inflates SEs; consider dropping/combining

medium.hint: Next step: spot the redundancy — near-twins split one credit, starving each of significance.
medium.explanation: Collinearity balloons variances: SEs ×~3 at r = 0.95 (VIF ≈ 10).
medium.deepDive: Step 1: VIF = 1/(1−0.95²) ≈ 10.26. Step 2: SEs inflate √10.26 ≈ 3.2×: t = 3.0 → 0.94 (n.s.). Step 3: Joint F still screams (shared signal real). Step 4: Fix: drop one twin, average them, or penalize (ridge).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Near-duplicate columns are a problem, not perfection.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: More redundancy worsens VIF further.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Inseparable twins can't get individual causal credit.

medium.prompt: Why not fit ordinary linear regression to a 0/1 outcome?

choices.label: B
choices.body: It can predict probabilities below 0 or above 1 and assumes constant variance

medium.hint: Next step: extend the line past the data — it must cross 0 and 1 eventually.
medium.explanation: Unbounded lines break probability bounds; Bernoulli variance p(1−p) isn't constant.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Fit: p̂ = −0.2 + 0.15×hours. Step 2: At 0h: −0.2 < 0; at 9h: 1.15 > 1 — impossible. Step 3: True variance peaks at p = 0.5 (0.25), vanishes at edges — fan pattern. Step 4: Logistic fixes both: bounded S plus proper likelihood.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Legal but misspecified — bounds and variance break.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Lines slope fine; they just overshoot [0,1].
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: x values exist; the outcome scale is the issue.

medium.prompt: A logistic model gives odds ratio 2.0 for tutoring (yes vs no). Correct reading?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Tutored students' ODDS of passing double (p 0.5→0.667, not 1.0)

medium.hint: Next step: convert — odds = p/(1−p); doubling odds isn't doubling p.
medium.explanation: OR = 2 multiplies odds; probability gains depend on baseline.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: Baseline p = 0.5: odds 1 → 2, so p = 2/3 ≈ 0.667. Step 2: Baseline p = 0.1: odds 0.111 → 0.222, p ≈ 0.182 (not 0.2). Step 3: Only tiny baselines approximate doubling. Step 4: Report with a baseline: '0.50 → 0.67'.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 0.5 doubling to 1.0 confuses odds with probability.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: ORs are multiplicative odds, never guaranteed counts.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: They match only near p ≈ 0.

medium.prompt: Slope is 0.8 with all 21 points but −0.2 without point P. What should you report?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Both fits, plus investigation of P (error? special case?) and robust alternatives

medium.hint: Next step: interrogate P before choosing — sign flips demand transparency.
medium.explanation: One point reversing the conclusion must be disclosed and stress-tested, not hidden.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: With P: +0.8 (CI 0.3-1.3). Step 2: Without: −0.2 (CI −0.6-0.2). Step 3: Check P: data-entry 999 vs real monopoly town? Step 4: Report both + robust slope (e.g., 0.1) so readers see the fragility.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Blind loyalty to n = 21 hides knife-edge fragility.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Silent deletion is misconduct-adjacent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Averaging estimates is not a statistical procedure.

hard.prompt: A histogram of commute times shows clear peaks near 15 minutes and near 55 minutes with a valley between. What is the best interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Right skew from one long tail

choices.label: B
choices.body: Two subgroups, e.g., local vs long-distance commuters

choices.label: D
choices.body: Proof the mean is the best center

hard.hint: Next step: ask what process makes two humps — one peak usually means one group.
hard.explanation: Two distinct peaks suggest a mixture of two groups rather than one skewed population.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Suppose 60 locals average 15 min and 40 express-train riders average 55 min. Step 2: The combined histogram stacks both mounds, with the valley near 35 min where few people fall. Step 3: The overall mean near 31 min describes nobody well. Step 4: So the right move is to split by group before summarizing center.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: One long tail makes a single peak with a slope, not two peaks with a valley.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A single symmetric group gives one central mound, not two separated humps.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A valley between peaks warns the single-mean summary may mislead, not that it is best.

hard.prompt: A town of 10 households each earning $60k gets one billionaire with $100M income. What happens to mean vs median?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Mean jumps to about $9.1M while median stays $60k

hard.hint: Next step: recompute each center with the newcomer — the median only cares about middle rank.
hard.explanation: One extreme moves the total hugely (mean) but only shifts middle order by half a slot (median).
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Old total is 10($60k) = $600k. Step 2: New total is $100.6M over 11 households, so the mean is about $9.15M. Step 3: Ordered incomes still have $60k in the middle (6th of 11). Step 4: The mean multiplied 150-fold while the typical household is unchanged — the mean-is-always-best reflex fails here.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The median resists: ten of eleven values are still $60k, so the middle stays $60k.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The median barely moves with one added extreme; it is the mean that explodes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The mean must absorb the full $100M added to the total.

hard.prompt: Two classes both have test-score range 40 points. Class A clusters near the mean (SD 5) while B spreads evenly (SD 12). What follows?

choices.label: B
choices.body: B is more spread out; range missed the clustering difference

choices.label: C
choices.body: A is more spread out because smaller SD means larger spread

choices.label: D
choices.body: SD is meaningless when ranges are equal

hard.hint: Next step: remember range sees only two points — ask what the other 28 students do.
hard.explanation: Equal ranges can hide different clustering; SD uses every deviation and exposes it.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Both classes span, say, 60 to 100. Step 2: In A, 28 of 30 scores sit within 75-85, so squared deviations average 25 and SD = 5. Step 3: In B the same range is filled evenly, squared deviations average 144 and SD = 12. Step 4: Same endpoints, very different typical deviations — SD tells the fuller story.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Matching endpoints do not imply matching interiors.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Smaller SD means tighter clustering, i.e., less spread, not more.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: SD remains the informative contrast exactly when ranges tie.

hard.prompt: A boxplot shows whiskers to 10 and 90 with flagged points at 120 and 150. What do the flagged points mean?

choices.label: A
choices.body: They are impossible and must be deleted

choices.label: B
choices.body: They lie beyond the whisker fences and deserve investigation

choices.label: D
choices.body: They prove the data are symmetric

hard.hint: Next step: recall whiskers stop at the last in-fence value — points beyond are plotted individually.
hard.explanation: Flagged points exceed the fence reach, marking candidate outliers to check, not auto-delete.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: With Q1 = 30, Q3 = 70, IQR = 40, the upper fence is 70 + 1.5(40) = 130. Step 2: The whisker stops at the largest value within 130 (here 90). Step 3: Values 120 and 150 plot as individual dots beyond it. Step 4: Each could be an error or a genuine extreme — the plot flags, the analyst decides.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Flagged points may be valid extremes; deletion without checking biases results.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Quartiles are the box edges (30/70 here), not the distant dots.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Far high dots with no low counterparts signal asymmetry, not symmetry.

hard.prompt: A $200 grocery bill appears in a dataset of $20-$60 weekly bills. It turns out to be a real stock-up trip, correctly recorded. What should the analyst do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Delete it silently to clean the data

choices.label: B
choices.body: Keep it and use resistant summaries or report with/without it

hard.hint: Next step: ask whether the value is an error or real — real extremes carry information.
hard.explanation: Valid extremes should not be silently dropped; show resistant summaries or both analyses.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Suppose 20 bills average $40 ($800 total) plus the $200 trip = $1000 over 21 bills. Step 2: Mean with it is $47.6, without it $40.0 — a $7.6 swing. Step 3: Median stays near $40 either way. Step 4: Reporting median plus mean-with-and-without keeps the real spending visible without letting one trip dominate.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Silent deletion hides $200 of genuine spending and biases totals downward.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Deleting everything above $50 discards legitimate upper-quarter data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Mean-substitution fabricates a value and understates variation.

hard.prompt: Adding one extreme high value to a dataset changes the mean a lot but the median barely. What does this show?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Mean and median are equally sensitive

choices.label: B
choices.body: The mean is sensitive to outliers; the median resists them

choices.label: D
choices.body: The median is always wrong with outliers

hard.hint: Next step: track what each formula uses — the mean spends every dollar, the median only ranks.
hard.explanation: The mean absorbs the full extreme in its total; the median only shifts middle rank.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Nine values of 10 total 90; mean = median = 10. Step 2: Add 100: total 190 over 10 values, mean 19. Step 3: Ordered list's middle is still 10 (median unchanged). Step 4: A 90% mean jump with zero median movement proves the sensitivity gap.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The worked example moves the mean 9 points and the median 0 — not equal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The mean moved from 10 to 19, so summaries are affected.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The median stayed exactly right at the typical value 10.

hard.prompt: Heights are roughly normal with mean 170 cm, SD 8 cm. Someone 188 cm tall (z ≈ 2.25) is…
hard.hint: Next step: convert to z, then recall ~2 SDs marks the top ~2.5%.
hard.explanation: z = (188−170)/8 = 2.25 puts this person near the 99th percentile.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Gap is 18 cm; divide by 8 cm to get z = 2.25. Step 2: About 97.7% of a normal curve falls below z = 2. Step 3: At z = 2.25 roughly 98.8% falls below. Step 4: Taller than ~99 of 100 people counts as genuinely unusual, not average.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Average would be z near 0 (170 cm), not 2.25 SDs up.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Positive z is above the mean, so shorter is backwards.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: z-scores have no cap at 2; extremes just grow rarer.

hard.prompt: To avoid being fooled the way Simpson's paradox fools pooled comparisons, what should an analyst do?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Compare within relevant groups and report stratified plus pooled rates

choices.label: D
choices.body: Average the group rates without weighting

hard.hint: Next step: stratify first — compute the comparison inside each group, then decide if pooling is fair.
hard.explanation: Stratified analysis exposes confounding; report both levels and pool only when groups are comparable.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Compute Ward-X and Ward-Y effects separately (e.g., +10 and +10 points). Step 2: Check group sizes per arm (90/10 vs 10/90 reveals the imbalance). Step 3: A size-weighted pooled gap of −14 points contradicts both strata, flagging confounding. Step 4: The honest report leads with strata and warns the pooled number mixes unlike patients.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Blind pooling is precisely the move that creates the paradox.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Deleting data hides the mechanism and wastes information.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Unweighted averaging of rates mis-weights groups and can preserve the distortion.

hard.prompt: A histogram shows most values bunched at the left with a long staircase trailing to high values. Which summary pair fits best?
hard.hint: Next step: name the shape first — bunch-left with high trail means right skew, so reach for resistant tools.
hard.explanation: Right skew calls for median and IQR, which the tail cannot drag.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Picture 80 values near 10-20 plus 5 values near 100. Step 2: Median stays near 15; IQR spans roughly 10-20. Step 3: Mean inflates toward 20+ and SD balloons past 15 from five points. Step 4: Resistant pair reports the bulk honestly where mean/SD echo the tail.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Mean/SD inherit the tail's pull in skewed data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Mode plus range wastes the middle 50% and spotlights extremes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Range is the least resistant spread, worst for skewed data.

hard.prompt: P(rain Sat) = 0.6, P(rain Sun) = 0.5, P(rain both days) = 0.4. What is P(no rain either day)?
hard.hint: Next step: find P(rain at least one day) first, then complement it.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Union = 0.6 + 0.5 − 0.4 = 0.7 (70 weekends in 100 see some rain). Step 2: Neither-day is the complement of that union. Step 3: 1 − 0.7 = 0.3. Step 4: About 30 of 100 weekends stay dry both days.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's the union (rain at least once), before complementing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's 1 minus the union's parts added wrongly, not 1 − 0.7.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's the both-days overlap, not the neither-days complement.

hard.prompt: 70% of students study; 80% of studiers pass and 30% of non-studiers pass. What is P(study AND pass)?
hard.hint: Next step: walk the tree branch — P(study) times P(pass | study).
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Of 100 students, 70 study. Step 2: 80% of those 70 pass: 56 students. Step 3: So 56 of 100 both study and pass. Step 4: (The overall pass rate adds the other branch: 0.56 + 0.30×0.30 = 0.65, but that union is not asked for.)

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's P(pass | study), only the second branch factor.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's the total pass rate over both branches, not the study-pass joint.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's P(no-study ∩ pass) = 0.30×0.30, the wrong branch.

hard.prompt: A pollster samples 2 voters from a town of 10,000 with 50% support. Why is P(both support) ≈ 0.5·0.5?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Because 10,000 is large, removal barely changes the mix

choices.label: B
choices.body: Because any two voters are clones

choices.label: D
choices.body: Because sampling needs replacement to be valid

hard.hint: Next step: check how much one draw changes the remaining share.
hard.explanation: Removing 1 of 10,000 barely moves 50%, so draws act nearly independent.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: After one supporter is drawn, 4,999 of 9,999 remain ≈ 0.49995. Step 2: Joint = 0.5 × 0.49995 ≈ 0.249975 vs 0.25 independent. Step 3: The gap is 0.000025 — negligible. Step 4: From a town of 10 this would fail (0.5×4/9≈0.222), but at 10,000 the without-replacement correction vanishes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Voters still vary; near-independence comes from population size, not cloning.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Exact equality needs replacement or infinite population; this is approximate.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Without-replacement sampling is valid; largeness just makes it mimic independence.

hard.prompt: A DNA match has P(match | innocent) = 1 in a million. A suspect matches in a city of 5 million. Why is P(innocent | match) NOT 1 in a million?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Because ~5 innocents are expected to match, so most matches are innocent

choices.label: C
choices.body: Because 5 million is less than a million

hard.hint: Next step: multiply the tiny rate by the huge pool — rare per-person can be common somewhere.
hard.explanation: About 5 innocent matches are expected among 5M people, so a match alone hardly proves guilt.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Expected innocent matches ≈ 5,000,000 × 1/1,000,000 = 5. Step 2: Add the 1 true culprit: ~6 matches citywide. Step 3: P(guilty | match) ≈ 1/6 ≈ 17%, so P(innocent | match) ≈ 83%. Step 4: Confusing P(match|innocent) with P(innocent|match) is the prosecutor's fallacy.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: No lab error is assumed; innocent matches arise by chance across millions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 5 million exceeds a million five-fold — that is exactly the point.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A match is evidence with a 5-to-1 innocent-to-guilty ratio here, not proof.

hard.prompt: Two urns: Urn 1 (70% of draws) holds 1 red/9 blue; Urn 2 holds 8 red/2 blue. You draw blue. What is P(Urn 1 | blue)?
hard.hint: Next step: total up blue draws from each urn, then take Urn 1's share.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Of 100 draws, 70 come from Urn 1 → 63 blue. Step 2: 30 from Urn 2 → 6 blue. Step 3: Blue total = 69, Urn-1 share 63/69 ≈ 0.913. Step 4: Blue evidence strongly favors the urn that rains blue, lifting 70% prior to ~91%.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That inverts the evidence; blue points toward Urn 1, not away.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's the prior; blue evidence pushes it up to ~91%.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Equal odds ignore both the 70/30 urn mix and the 9:1 vs 1:4 blue rates.

hard.prompt: A casino game pays $10 with probability 0.05 per play, else $0. Over 10,000 plays the casino expects to pay out about…
hard.hint: Next step: find the mean payout per play, then scale by plays.
hard.explanation: Mean per play = 10×0.05 = $0.50; over 10,000 plays ≈ $5,000.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Per-play expectation: $10(0.05) + $0(0.95) = $0.50. Step 2: Linearity of expectation scales it: 10,000 × $0.50. Step 3: That equals $5,000 expected payout. Step 4: Individual streaks swing wildly, but the 10,000-play total hugs $5,000 by the law of large numbers.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is the 100-play expectation, off by 100×.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That would need a $5 average per play — 10× too high.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That would need $10 average per play — 20× too high.

hard.prompt: Lottery players avoid past winning numbers, saying those are 'used up'. With 1,000,000 equally likely tickets each draw, what is true?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Past winners are less likely next draw

choices.label: B
choices.body: Each draw is independent: past winners keep probability 1/1,000,000

choices.label: D
choices.body: Avoiding winners raises your jackpot share only if you win

hard.hint: Next step: check the draw mechanism — new balls, same million combos.
hard.explanation: Independent draws reset odds; every combination holds 1/1,000,000 each time.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: The machine holds no memory of last week's balls. Step 2: P(last week's combo again) = 1/1,000,000, same as any unplayed combo. Step 3: Over a million draws each combo appears ~once on average — including repeats. Step 4: Avoiding winners changes nothing about winning odds (crowding effects aside).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 'Used up' implies sampling without replacement across draws; draws replace fully.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Unplayed combos share the identical 1/1,000,000 chance.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Shared-prize strategy is a separate payout question, not a probability edge.

hard.prompt: A die is rolled 4 times. What is P(at least one six)?
hard.hint: Next step: 'at least one' signals complement — find P(no sixes) first.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Per roll P(no six) = 5/6. Step 2: Independence across 4 rolls: (5/6)^4 = 625/1296 ≈ 0.4823. Step 3: Complement: 1 − 0.4823 = 0.5177. Step 4: Just over half of 4-roll windows show a six.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Adding 1/6 four times double-counts multi-six windows.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's P(six on one specified roll), not across four.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's P(all four are sixes) ≈ 0.00077, the opposite extreme.

hard.prompt: Event A: 'die shows 1 or 2'. Event B: 'die shows 2 or 3'. Are they disjoint? Independent?
hard.hint: Next step: first list shared outcomes, then test the product rule.
hard.explanation: They share {2} so not disjoint; P(A∩B)=1/6 ≈ 0.167 vs (1/3)(1/3)=1/9 ≈ 0.111, so dependent.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: A = {1,2}, B = {2,3}: outcome 2 sits in both — overlap exists. Step 2: P(A)=P(B)=2/6=1/3; product = 1/9 ≈ 0.111. Step 3: Actual joint P({2}) = 1/6 ≈ 0.167. Step 4: Joint exceeds product, so knowing A (2 possible, one shared) raises B's chance — positive dependence.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Sharing outcome 2 kills disjointness and the product test fails.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: They do overlap on {2}, so 'disjoint' is wrong.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Overlap with joint ≠ product means dependence, not independence.

hard.prompt: To halve the standard error, what must happen to n (all else equal)?
hard.hint: Next step: use SE ∝ 1/√n — halving needs √n to double.
hard.explanation: SE halves when √n doubles, i.e., n × 4.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: SE = σ/√n. Step 2: Want σ/√(n_new) = (1/2)σ/√n. Step 3: So √(n_new) = 2√n, giving n_new = 4n. Step 4: E.g., SE 2 at n = 25 becomes 1 at n = 100 — precision is quadratically expensive.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Doubling n cuts SE by only 1/√2 ≈ 0.71, not half.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Smaller n inflates SE.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Adding a constant shifts √n negligibly at large n.

hard.prompt: Averages of 50 dice rolls look bell-shaped around 3.5, though single rolls are flat. Why?

choices.label: B
choices.body: CLT: averaging 50 independent bounded rolls yields near-normal means

choices.label: C
choices.body: The uniform distribution is secretly normal

hard.hint: Next step: count the averaging — 50 rolls per mean is heavy CLT territory.
hard.explanation: Mean of 50 iid rolls: E = 3.5, SE ≈ 1.708/√50 ≈ 0.24, nearly normal.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Single-roll SD = √(35/12) ≈ 1.708. Step 2: Mean of 50 has SE ≈ 1.708/7.07 ≈ 0.242. Step 3: Bounded iid summands satisfy CLT fast; n = 50 suffices. Step 4: Observed means land 3.02-3.98 (~±2 SE) about 95% of the time.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Grouping changes no physics; only the statistic changes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Flat single rolls stay flat; only their average bell-shapes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 3.5 is the center of a ±0.24 scatter, not a guarantee.

hard.prompt: Sample: n = 12 salaries with two extreme CEO outliers. A classmate runs a z-interval via CLT. What's wrong?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Tiny n plus extreme outliers: x̄'s distribution is still skewed; use median/bootstrap or get more data

hard.hint: Next step: check both pillars — n = 12 is small AND outliers signal heavy skew.
hard.explanation: CLT hasn't kicked in at n = 12 with extremes; normal approximation for x̄ fails.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Two $5M salaries among ten $60k ones: mean ≈ $905k, median $60k. Step 2: x̄'s sampling distribution inherits the skew at n = 12. Step 3: z critical values then misstate coverage badly. Step 4: Median intervals or log-scale analysis behave far better here.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: No universal small-n cutoff exists; skew and outliers raise the bar.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Outliers may be genuine CEOs — the issue is method, not fraud.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: z has no maximum-n rule; it has a large-enough-n requirement.

hard.prompt: True p = 0.5. How large must n be so the 95% margin for p̂ is at most ±2 points?
hard.hint: Next step: solve 1.96√(0.25/n) ≤ 0.02 for n.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Worst-case p(1−p) = 0.25 at p = 0.5. Step 2: 1.96√(0.25/n) ≤ 0.02 ⇒ √(0.25/n) ≤ 0.0102. Step 3: 0.25/n ≤ 0.000104 ⇒ n ≥ 2401. Step 4: Halving margin from ±4 (n≈600) to ±2 quadruples n — the square-root price again.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: n = 500 gives ±4.4 points, over twice too wide.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: n = 100 gives ±9.8 points.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: n = 10000 gives ±0.98 points — needlessly precise here.

hard.prompt: A bootstrap distribution of the median from 2000 replicates is itself strongly right-skewed. What interval should you report?

choices.label: B
choices.body: The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap medians

choices.label: C
choices.body: Median ± 2 SD of the raw data

choices.label: D
choices.body: A single point: the observed median

hard.hint: Next step: let the replicates speak — cut off the outer 5% where they actually fall.
hard.explanation: Percentile method reads quantiles off the bootstrap distribution, skew and all.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Sort the 2000 medians: say 2.5th = $48k, 97.5th = $72k. Step 2: Report ($48k, $72k) — asymmetric around $55k, reflecting real skew. Step 3: Symmetric ±2SE would force ($41k, $69k), understating upside. Step 4: Percentiles adapt; formulas assume.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Symmetric formula ignores the very skew the bootstrap revealed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Raw-data SD describes individuals, not the median's uncertainty.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A point estimate reports no uncertainty at all.

hard.prompt: Why does bootstrapping typically FAIL for the sample maximum?

choices.label: B
choices.body: The max of a resample can never exceed the observed max, so it misses upside

hard.hint: Next step: ask what values a with-replacement resample can contain — only observed ones.
hard.explanation: Resamples draw from observed data, so their maxima pile at/below the sample max.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Sample max = 97 from n = 30. Step 2: Every replicate's max ≤ 97 (values only repeat). Step 3: The bootstrap distribution stacks at 97, blind to population values like 110. Step 4: Percentile intervals then under-cover the true max — smoothness/extrapolation methods are needed.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Resample size equals n by construction; size isn't the flaw.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Maxima follow extreme-value laws, not normal ones.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Computation is trivial; the statistical logic is what's broken.

hard.prompt: A student says 'with n = 10,000 our incomes became normally distributed'. What's the error?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Confusing the sampling distribution of x̄ with the raw data distribution

hard.hint: Next step: separate what got normal — the average's behavior, not people's paychecks.
hard.explanation: Large n normalizes the mean's distribution; raw incomes keep their skew.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: 10,000 incomes still show the long right tail (median ~$60k, mean ~$85k). Step 2: Their average x̄ ≈ $85k ± σ/100 — nearly normal around μ. Step 3: One bell (x̄'s) tightens; the other (incomes') never moves. Step 4: Claiming the data 'became normal' mistakes the statistic for the sample.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Big samples are routine in administrative data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 10,000 is plenty for x̄'s normality; size isn't the issue.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Many variables are near-normal; the claim's error is about WHICH distribution.

hard.prompt: Two sampling distributions of x̄, both n = 50: pop A σ = 10, pop B σ = 30. How do they compare?

choices.label: B
choices.body: B's is 3× wider (SE 4.24 vs 1.41), both centered on their μ

hard.hint: Next step: compute each SE — same n means σ drives the width.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: √50 ≈ 7.07. Step 2: 10/7.07 ≈ 1.41; 30/7.07 ≈ 4.24. Step 3: Ratio 4.24/1.41 = 3 = σ ratio. Step 4: Each centers on its own μ — sampling distributions inherit location from their population, width from σ/√n.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Same n cannot equalize different σs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Larger σ means wider, not narrower.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Centers are μ_A and μ_B, not 0 (that's z-scores).

hard.prompt: Lognormal mass incomes: at n = 25 the 95% z-interval for μ covers only ~87%. What fixes coverage?
hard.hint: Next step: diagnose — skew breaks the normal approximation at n = 25, so feed CLT more data or transform.
hard.explanation: n = 25 is too small for lognormal skew; n ≈ 200+ (or log analysis) restores coverage.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Miss rate 13% vs nominal 5% — undercoverage of 8 points. Step 2: x̄'s right skew pushes misses asymmetrically (upper misses dominate). Step 3: At n = 250, skew falls ~3.2× and coverage nears 94%. Step 4: Alternatively log-transform (symmetric scale) or bootstrap-t — deleting data just biases μ downward.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Repeating the failing recipe preserves the 87% coverage.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Trimming the rich redefines μ downward — coverage of a new target, dishonestly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Lower confidence narrows further and worsens the miss rate.

hard.prompt: Two groups' 95% CIs for means overlap slightly: (10, 20) and (18, 28). Can you conclude the means differ insignificantly?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Yes, any overlap proves no difference

choices.label: B
choices.body: No — overlap of 95% CIs does not equal a 5% test of the difference; test μ₁−μ₂ directly

hard.hint: Next step: recall the difference has its own SE — smaller than the sum of margins suggests.
hard.explanation: SE of the difference is √(SE₁²+SE₂²), tighter than stacked margins; slight overlap can still be significant.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Each CI half-width ≈ 2·SE ≈ 5, so SE₁ ≈ SE₂ ≈ 2.5. Step 2: SE_diff = √(2.5²+2.5²) ≈ 3.54. Step 3: Difference = 23−15 = 8; z ≈ 8/3.54 ≈ 2.26 → p ≈ 0.024, significant. Step 4: Yet the intervals overlap on 18-20 — eyeballing overlap misleads; compute the difference CI (1.1, 14.9), which excludes 0.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Overlap rules of thumb are conservative and often wrong at the boundary.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Both intervals are valid summaries; the error is only in comparing them naively.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Overlap says nothing that precise; p here is ~0.02, far from 0.5.

hard.prompt: Two 95% CIs from the same sample: A uses s correctly (width 8); B ignores an outlier and reports width 5. Is B better?

choices.label: B
choices.body: No — B's width is dishonest if it hides real variation; coverage matters more than raw narrowness

hard.hint: Next step: ask what the width left out — valid precision keeps its coverage promise.
hard.explanation: A narrower interval that under-covers is worse; width without coverage is vanity.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Suppose the outlier is a genuine $2M salary among 30 at ~$60k. Step 2: Deleting it cuts s from $360k to $15k and SE from $66k to $2.8k. Step 3: B's (tight) interval then misses μ in ~40% of reruns vs 5% nominal. Step 4: Report A (or robust methods) — precision must be honest.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Narrower wins only at equal coverage; here coverage collapses.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Genuine extremes carry information; silent deletion biases.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Validity differs: one keeps its 95% promise, one breaks it.

hard.prompt: How large must n be for a 95% CI with margin ≤ 2 when σ ≈ 15 (use z*)?
hard.hint: Next step: solve 1.96·σ/√n ≤ 2 for n.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: 1.96 × 15 = 29.4. Step 2: 29.4/2 = 14.7. Step 3: 14.7² = 216.1, round up to 217 (225 with t-adjustment). Step 4: n = 60 would give margin ≈ 3.8 — nearly double the budget.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Margin at 60 is 1.96×15/√60 ≈ 3.80, too wide.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: n = 15 gives margin ≈ 7.6.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: n = 900 gives margin ≈ 0.98 — overkill costing 4× the data.

hard.prompt: Only 3 successes in n = 30 (p̂ = 0.10). Why is the Wald interval p̂ ± 1.96·SE risky here?

choices.label: B
choices.body: np̂ = 3 < 10: normal approximation fails and the interval can dip below 0

hard.hint: Next step: check successes and failures against 10.
hard.explanation: Failures = 27 pass but successes = 3 fail; sampling distribution skews and Wald mis-covers.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: SE = √(0.1×0.9/30) ≈ 0.0548; Wald gives 0.10 ± 0.107 = (−0.007, 0.207). Step 2: Negative proportions are impossible — a red flag. Step 3: True coverage here is ~85%, not 95%. Step 4: Use Wilson/plus-four: (0.035, 0.256)-ish, always inside [0,1].

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 3 successes is tiny, not large.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Proportions get intervals routinely once conditions hold.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 30 is modest; the 3 successes are the binding constraint.

hard.prompt: How many respondents are needed for a 95% margin of ±3 points (worst case)?
hard.hint: Next step: use p = 0.5 (max variance) and solve 1.96√(0.25/n) ≤ 0.03.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: 1.96/0.03 ≈ 65.33. Step 2: Squared ≈ 4269. Step 3: ×0.25 ≈ 1067. Step 4: ±2 points would need 2401 — tightening by a third costs 2.25× the interviews.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 363 gives ±5.1 points.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 1112 is the ±2.94-point nearby (n for 98%?) — overshoots slightly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 2401 is the ±2-point size — overkill here.

hard.prompt: When is the pooled-variance two-sample t-interval appropriate?

choices.label: B
choices.body: When both groups are independent random samples, near-normal, with plausibly equal variances

hard.hint: Next step: check the three pooled-t ingredients — independence, normality-ish, equal spread.
hard.explanation: Pooled sp² blends groups only if one common variance is believable.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: s₁ = 9.8, s₂ = 10.4, n = 25 each: ratio ≈ 1.06 — pooling fine. Step 2: If s₁ = 5, s₂ = 20 (ratio 4), pooled SE distorts; use Welch. Step 3: Paired data need the differences route instead. Step 4: Known variances call for z, not pooled t.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: With unequal variances pooling mis-weights and mis-covers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Pairs correlate within subject — independence fails.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Known σ removes the reason to pool sample variances.

hard.prompt: Why can a paired CI be much narrower than an unpaired CI on the same people?

choices.label: C
choices.body: Pairing removes the need for SE

hard.hint: Next step: decompose variance — person effects inflate group SDs but vanish in differences.
hard.explanation: Baseline weights vary hugely (SD 25 lb) while losses vary little (SD 6 lb); pairing works on losses.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Unpaired SE ≈ √(25²/30+25²/30) ≈ 6.45 → margin ≈ 13. Step 2: Paired SE = 6/√30 ≈ 1.10 → margin ≈ 2.2. Step 3: ~6× narrower from the same 30 people. Step 4: No new subjects needed — design, not size, did it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Same 30 people; pairing restructures, not duplicates.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SE = sd/√n stays central to the paired CI.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Unpaired is valid but wasteful when pairing is available.

hard.prompt: Before trusting a t-interval with n = 18, what plot check is most useful?

choices.label: B
choices.body: A histogram/dotplot of the data for skew and outliers

choices.label: C
choices.body: A bar chart of the alphabet

hard.hint: Next step: look at the data — shape violations show up visually at small n.
hard.explanation: One outlier or strong skew at n = 18 warns that x̄ isn't t-shaped yet.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Dotplot shows 17 values near 20 plus one at 200. Step 2: That single point owns ~50% of the total — x̄'s distribution skews hard. Step 3: t criticals then mis-cover. Step 4: Barrett: transform, use median CI, or gather more data.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: IDs carry no shape information.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Letters are irrelevant to numeric shape.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: At n = 18 the CLT hasn't earned blind trust — look first.

hard.prompt: Same data, same SE = 2: 95% CI uses 1.96, 99% uses 2.576. How much wider is the 99% interval?
hard.hint: Next step: ratio the critical values — same SE cancels.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: 95% margin = 1.96×2 = 3.92. Step 2: 99% margin = 2.576×2 = 5.152. Step 3: 5.152/3.92 ≈ 1.314. Step 4: Four extra coverage points (95→99) cost nearly a third more width.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The multiplier visibly changes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 4× width would need z* ≈ 7.8 (≈100% coverage).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Higher confidence widens — never narrows.

hard.prompt: A two-sided test gives p = 0.08. For the matching one-sided test in the observed direction, p is…
hard.hint: Next step: picture the two tails — one-sided keeps only the observed side.
hard.explanation: Two-sided splits α across both tails; one-sided concentrates on one, halving p when direction matches.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: z = 1.75: two-sided p = 2×P(Z ≥ 1.75) ≈ 2×0.0401 = 0.0802. Step 2: One-sided (correct direction): P(Z ≥ 1.75) ≈ 0.0401. Step 3: Same data, same z — only the question's tail count changed. Step 4: Choosing sides after seeing data doubles the real error rate, so pre-specify direction.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Doubling goes the wrong way; one-sided narrows to one tail.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 0.92 is P(Z < 1.75)-style complement confusion.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Tail count directly scales p; it can't stay put.

hard.prompt: Lowering α from 0.05 to 0.01 (same n, same effect) does what to error rates?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Cuts both Type I and Type II

choices.label: B
choices.body: Cuts Type I but raises Type II (lowers power)

hard.hint: Next step: picture the rejection bar rising — fewer alarms of any kind.
hard.explanation: A stricter bar means fewer false alarms but more missed real effects.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Rejection needs |z| > 2.58 instead of 1.96. Step 2: True-null false alarms fall 5% → 1%. Step 3: A real effect with z ≈ 2.2 now fails to clear — power might drop 0.65 → 0.35. Step 4: The only free fix is more n, shrinking SE so both errors can fall.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: One cutoff can't improve both — the tradeoff is fundamental at fixed n.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The bar plainly moved; rates must respond.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Type I falls by construction.

hard.prompt: To raise power from 0.50 to 0.90 for the same effect and α, roughly how must n change?
hard.hint: Next step: recall z-behavior — pushing the noncentrality from ~1.96 to ~3.24 needs ~2.7× the √n multiple squared.
hard.explanation: Large power jumps are expensive: n must roughly triple.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Power 0.50 needs noncentrality ≈ z_{1−α/2} ≈ 1.96 (two-sided 5%). Step 2: Power 0.90 needs ≈ 1.96 + 1.28 = 3.24. Step 3: Ratio 3.24/1.96 ≈ 1.65; n scales with its square ≈ 2.73. Step 4: E.g., n = 64 → ~175 per group.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: +20% n lifts power only ~0.50 → ~0.57.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Halving n crashes power toward ~0.30.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: n is power's main lever via SE = σ/√n.

hard.prompt: A 2×3 table test needs expected counts ≥ 5, but one cell expects 1.2. What should you do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Run χ² anyway; tiny counts don't matter

choices.label: B
choices.body: Combine categories or use Fisher's exact test

hard.hint: Next step: recall the approximation's fuel — χ² needs enough expected count per cell.
hard.explanation: Sparse cells break the χ² approximation; merging or exact methods fix it.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Cell with E = 1.2 contributes (O−E)²/E with huge leverage per count. Step 2: The χ² curve then misstates tail odds. Step 3: Merging two columns lifts E to ~6 and restores validity. Step 4: Fisher's exact computes the true discrete tail without approximation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: E = 1.2 cells distort p badly — the rule exists for this case.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Silent deletion biases associations.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Fabricating counts corrupts every cell.

hard.prompt: χ² = 12.3 with df = 3 for independence. What follows (critical value 7.81 at 5%)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Fail to reject; variables look independent

hard.hint: Next step: compare statistic to cutoff — past it means reject.
hard.explanation: 12.3 > 7.81 lands in the rejection tail; association is significant.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: H₀ (independence) predicts χ² ≈ df = 3 on average. Step 2: 12.3 sits far out; P(χ²₃ ≥ 12.3) ≈ 0.006. Step 3: Only 6 reruns in 1000 look this lopsided under H₀. Step 4: Association ≠ causation — lurking variables may drive it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 12.3 clears 7.81, so H₀ falls.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: χ² shows association only, never causation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: df = 3 fits (2−1)(3−1) = 2 or 4-cat fit — not 12×3.

hard.prompt: Why not just run all pairwise t-tests instead of ANOVA for 5 groups?

choices.label: B
choices.body: 10 tests at 5% give ~40% family-wise false-alarm chance; ANOVA controls it

choices.label: D
choices.body: Pairwise tests are always more powerful

hard.hint: Next step: compound the error — 1 − 0.95^10.
hard.explanation: Multiple testing inflates overall Type I error; ANOVA's single gate keeps it at 5%.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: 5 groups → C(5,2) = 10 pairs. Step 2: P(≥1 false alarm) = 1 − 0.95^10 ≈ 0.401. Step 3: ~40% of all-equal experiments would 'find' something. Step 4: ANOVA screens at 5% first; Tukey-style post-hocs then hold the line.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: t-tests are valid singly; the sin is unadjusted repetition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: ANOVA assumes normality/equal variance too.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Unadjusted pairs buy fake power with real false alarms.

hard.prompt: Two studies of the same drug: A: effect 8 units, p = 0.04, CI (0.5, 15.5). B: effect 2 units, p = 0.001, CI (1.0, 3.0). Which shows the stronger effect?

choices.label: A
choices.body: B, smaller p means bigger effect

choices.label: B
choices.body: A: 8 units dwarfs 2, though less precisely estimated

hard.hint: Next step: compare point estimates and CIs — p mixes size with precision.
hard.explanation: Effect size lives in the estimate; p mixes it with sample size.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: A's CI centers 8 (wide: small n). Step 2: B's centers 2 (tight: huge n). Step 3: B's tiny p certifies its 2 units, not superiority. Step 4: For patients, 8 (uncertain) vs 2 (certain) is a real tradeoff p-values hide.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: p confounds magnitude with n — B just had more precision.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: p never decides magnitude.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: CIs are exactly what disentangle size from certainty.

hard.prompt: A team tests 50 foods against cancer, finds one with p = 0.03, and headlines it. What's wrong?

choices.label: B
choices.body: With 50 tests, ~2-3 false hits are expected under global null; one p = 0.03 is unsurprising

hard.hint: Next step: count the swings — 50 tests at 5% breed false positives.
hard.explanation: Expected false positives ≈ 50×0.05 = 2.5; cherry-picking one is p-hacking.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Under all-null, P(≥1 p < 0.05) = 1 − 0.95^50 ≈ 0.923. Step 2: Over 92% of such fishing trips 'find' something. Step 3: The headline reports the minimum of 50 p-values as if it were one test. Step 4: Pre-registration plus Bonferroni/FDR correction is the honest route.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: p < 0.05 from the luckiest of 50 is not 5% evidence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Food studies are fine — undisclosed multiplicity is the flaw.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 0.03 is publishable singly; the 50 hidden tests are the issue.

hard.prompt: Family-wise error rate (FWER) vs false discovery rate (FDR): which statement is right?

choices.label: B
choices.body: FWER controls P(any false rejection); FDR controls expected share of false rejections among rejections

hard.hint: Next step: parse the names — 'any' (family) vs 'share among discoveries'.
hard.explanation: FWER guards against even one false hit; FDR tolerates a controlled fraction among hits.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: 1000 gene tests, 50 rejections: FWER 5% means P(≥1 false among 50) ≤ 0.05. Step 2: FDR 5% means E[false/50] ≤ 0.05 (~2-3 false OK). Step 3: FDR (Benjamini-Hochberg) thus rejects more — power for screens. Step 4: Confirmatory trials want FWER; exploratory screens accept FDR.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That defines FWER, not FDR.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Different targets: any-vs-share.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: FWER (Bonferroni) is stricter; FDR trades strictness for discoveries.

hard.prompt: Why does least squares minimize SQUARED residuals rather than absolute ones?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Squares penalize big misses disproportionately and give a unique smooth (calculus-friendly) solution

hard.hint: Next step: compare penalties — |10| vs 10² — and ask which yields one clean minimum.
hard.explanation: Quadratic loss is differentiable with a closed-form solution; it also weights large errors heavily.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Misses of 1 and 9: absolute total 10; squared total 1 + 81 = 82 — the 9 dominates. Step 2: The squared criterion Σ(y−ŷ)² is smooth, so derivatives give the normal equations. Step 3: Solution: b = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy — unique when XᵀX inverts. Step 4: Absolute loss is robust but non-smooth (median-style, iterative) — a different tool.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The square drives the entire derivation, not decor.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Absolute residuals are zero only at perfect fits.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Squares amplify outliers — the known price of LS, not ignorance.

hard.prompt: Adding a 5th predictor to a regression with n = 30 will, in-sample, tend to…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Never lower R² (even for pure noise); adjusted R² penalizes the addition

hard.hint: Next step: ask if R² can fall when the optimizer may simply set the new coefficient to 0.
hard.explanation: Extra predictors can only help fit the sample (or tie); adjusted R² guards the comparison.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Old best: R² = 0.50. Step 2: New coefficient free: optimizer keeps 0.50 or better — say 0.53 with noise. Step 3: Adjusted R² = 1 − (1−R²)(n−1)/(n−p−1): 0.50→adj ~0.43 vs 0.53→adj ~0.43 — no real gain. Step 4: Out-of-sample, noise predictors usually hurt.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: R² is monotone non-decreasing in predictors, in-sample.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Noise variables are usually insignificant.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Perfect fit needs ~n orthogonal predictors, not one noise column.

hard.prompt: Residual spread grows from ±2 at low x to ±10 at high x (fan shape). What should you do?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Use weighted least squares or transform y (e.g., log); ordinary SEs/p-values mislead

hard.hint: Next step: name it — heteroscedasticity — then fix the variance, not the data.
hard.explanation: Fan residuals violate constant variance; inference assuming it understates high-x uncertainty.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Variance ratio ≈ 25 (10²/2²). Step 2: Ordinary 95% intervals at high x cover ~75% — undercoverage. Step 3: Log(y) stabilizes: spread ±0.15 across x. Step 4: Or weight by 1/variance; deleting data biases the slope instead.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: ±2 → ±10 is textbook non-constant variance.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: High-x points are informative; downweight, don't discard.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: More low-x data never fixes high-x variance.

hard.prompt: Why does extrapolation fail even when the in-sample fit is near-perfect?

choices.label: B
choices.body: New x-regions can bring new mechanisms (saturation, thresholds) invisible in-range

hard.hint: Next step: think dose-response — linear at low doses, toxic/saturating past a threshold.
hard.explanation: In-range data cannot identify regime changes it never observed.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Fertilizer 0-50 kg: +2 bu/kg, R² = 0.99. Step 2: At 200 kg salt toxicity crashes yield — outside all training data. Step 3: Line predicts +400 bu; field shows −50. Step 4: Mechanisms (chemistry), not math, set the boundary.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Generalization needs same-regime assumption, never automatic.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Zero in-sample residuals say nothing out-of-range.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Extension is allowed — and often wrong.

hard.prompt: Which prediction is interpolation (safer) vs extrapolation (riskier)? Data: x in [10, 20].
hard.hint: Next step: place each x against [10, 20] — inside vs outside decides.
hard.explanation: Inside-range predictions borrow nearby evidence; outside-range bets on persistence.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: x = 15: neighbors at 14, 16 anchor it — SE of fit small. Step 2: x = 40: 20 units past the edge — SE of prediction balloons (leverage). Step 3: Prediction interval at 40 is ~3× wider than at 15. Step 4: Same line, very different trust.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Reversed: 15 sits inside, 40 far outside.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Distance from data plainly differentiates them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 15 enjoys dense local support; risk differs.

hard.prompt: A randomized trial assigns 500 patients to drug/placebo and finds +10 recovery points (p < 0.001). Why is causal language justified here?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Randomization balances known and unknown confounders in expectation

hard.hint: Next step: ask what randomization buys — comparable groups except treatment.
hard.explanation: Random assignment severs treatment from background causes, isolating the causal effect.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Age, severity, genetics split ~50/50 by the coin. Step 2: Only the pill differs systematically. Step 3: So the +10 gap (CI 6-14) estimates the causal effect. Step 4: p quantifies surprise under no-effect; design (not p) licenses 'causes'.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Size gives precision; randomization gives comparability.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: p measures evidence, never mechanisms.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Trials can err (5% at α) — design just makes errors quantified.

hard.prompt: Towns with more storks have more babies (r = 0.8). A council funds stork nests to raise birth rates. Error?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Ecological/confounded association (rural towns differ) mistaken for causation; nests won't cause babies

hard.hint: Next step: compare town types — rural vs urban explains both counts.
hard.explanation: Third variables (area type, housing) drive both; intervening on storks changes nothing.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Rural towns: 50 storks, 200 babies; urban: 2 storks, 40 babies. Step 2: Within rural towns, storks vs babies r ≈ 0. Step 3: The 0.8 lives between town-types, not within them. Step 4: Nest funding buys birds, not babies — classic ecological fallacy.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Large r never converts observation into causation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Stork habits are irrelevant; confounding is the charge.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 0.8 is large — and still only associational.

hard.prompt: Model A (3 predictors): R² = 0.60. Model B (adds 2 noise vars): R² = 0.605. Which predicts new data better, likely?

choices.label: B
choices.body: A, likely: B's gain is probably overfit noise; compare adjusted R²/CV error

hard.hint: Next step: penalize complexity — in-sample R² always favors bigger models.
hard.explanation: In-sample fit rewards complexity; honest comparison adjusts or cross-validates.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Adjusted: A ≈ 1−0.40(99/96) ≈ 0.5875 (n = 100). Step 2: B ≈ 1−0.395(99/94) ≈ 0.5840 — the noise gain evaporates under penalty. Step 3: Judge by adjusted/CV, where fake gains vanish. Step 4: Typical CV: A MSE 100 vs B 104 — A generalizes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: In-sample R² is biased toward complexity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Adjusted/CV usually separates them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: R² is useful — with penalties.

hard.prompt: Cook's distance D = 1.8 for one point (rest < 0.1). What does that signal and what next?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Highly influential point: inspect it, check leverage/residual, consider robust fit or separate modeling

hard.hint: Next step: read D as overall fit-shift — above ~0.5-1 demands attention.
hard.explanation: D blends leverage and residual into one influence gauge; 1.8 dwarfs the rest.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: D > 1 flags major fit-shift on removal. Step 2: Decompose: x 4 SDs out + studentized residual 3.5. Step 3: Verify recording; try robust Huber fit (slope 0.8 → 0.35). Step 4: If genuine (e.g., valid market crash week), model it explicitly (indicator) rather than deleting.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: D is the standard influence diagnostic.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Deletion without documentation biases and hides fragility.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: More typical-x data dilutes leverage — often the real fix.
